items.title: Was Madrid F1 race an economic upgrade on Barcelona?
items.author: Samarth Kanal
items.content:
The inaugural 2026 Spanish Formula 1 Grand Prix at the Madring created €544 million in economic activity, supported 10,948 jobs, and generated €95m in tax revenue, according to its organiser.

The Madring is a part-street circuit built around the IFEMA conference centre - with the track layout set to be changed for 2027 to improve the quality of racing and frequency of overtaking.

The grand prix promoter ran a study conducted by PwC showing that, for every €1 of economic activity directly linked to the event, €4.60 was generated across Madrid’s wider economy.

The total economic impact was 16.5% larger than expected, the grand prix supported 23.7% more jobs than anticipated, and the overall tax contribution was 14.5% more than predicted.

In comparison to Madrid’s figure of €544m in economic activity for 2026, the Barcelona GP generated over €300m in local economic activity in 2024, according to its own reports. This was reaffirmed by Barcelona circuit CEO Pol Gilbert as part of the track’s recent extension announcement, where he said that “Formula 1 generates an economic impact of more than €300 million per edition” at the venue.

F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali recently said the US GP at Austin generated “over $1 billion” for the local area in 2026, while the Las Vegas GP has generated over $3.2bn cumulatively for the local area over its three editions.

IFEMA Madrid chairman Jose Vicente de los Mozos said that the figures “confirm the strategic importance the Grand Prix has gained for Madrid’s economy and international profile from its very first edition, generating economic activity equivalent to 0.16% of the Madrid Region’s GDP and 0.30% of the city of Madrid’s GDP”.

The grand prix attracted 353,000 attendees. The survey estimates that 35% of visitors were from overseas and 20% travelling from elsewhere in Spain - meaning 45% were from Madrid and its immediate vicinity.

International visitors spent an average of €2,772 per person over the course of their stay - compared with €1,099 from Spanish visitors and €659 among Madrid residents - with those figures including the estimated average ticket price, which is not stated.

International visitors to the grand prix therefore spent 1.7 times that of an average international tourist to Madrid, and 2.9 times more than an international tourist visiting Spain. Domestic visitors spent 3.8 times more than a domestic tourist would on a trip to the Madrid region.

Local digital publication Democrata found that hotel prices averaged €485 - 70% more than usual - for the grand prix.

Around 49% of visitors stayed in hotels, 32% in short-term rental accommodation, and 19% with family and friends - generating €95m in tax revenues.

Short-term rentals have been a contentious issue for the local area in recent years as, in 2025, the Spanish government cracked down on Airbnbs, removing nearly 66,000 listings across the country and fining the company €64m for illegal listings.

Furthermore, residents local to the Madring protested its environmental and societal impact, including noise concerns.

The survey found that 95.3% of international attendees said the grand prix had ‘enhanced Madrid’s international image’ and 98.1% would recommend Madrid as a tourist destination, with 86% of attendees saying they were likely to return.

PwC partner Jordi Esteve said: “Through extensive fieldwork, we have found that grand prix visitors spend more and stay longer than the average visitor. This is helping Madrid attract high-value tourism, generating greater economic activity and supporting employment.”

PwC conducted 1,102 face-to-face surveys between the Friday and Sunday of the race weekend.

items.title: New Pogačar Documentary ‘POG1’: Before the Yellow Jerseys Came the Socks
items.author: ahood
items.content: Colnago’s 'POG1: The Making of a Legend' premieres November 13 on YouTube. Tadej Pogačar’s parents, partner and mentor tell the story of his meteoric rise.
items.lbText:
Another Pogačar documentary drops this week and dives into his roots. (Photo: Gruber Images)

Long before he was dominating the Tour de France, Tadej Pogačar was spending his birthday money on socks and sunglasses.

That’s according to POG1: The Making of a Legend , a new documentary that drops this week from Colnago Cultura.

The latest in a flurry of fresh Pogačar content, the documentary follows the Slovenian’s evolution from an unknown kid to a global phenomenon.

The director uses interviews with his parents, his partner Urška Žigart, longtime mentor Andrej Hauptman, teammates and ex-pros to tell the story of his rise to Tour de France dominance.

The documentary premieres Friday on Colnago’s YouTube channel and it’s free in every country.

Velo has only seen a few snippets, but this documentary dives into Pogačar’s origin story with new details and anecdotes.

Pogačar’s father recounts how his son followed his older brother into football and then cycling. Once the bike took over, it was clear to his parents that Little Pogi was obsessed.

“As soon as he started it became the only thing in the world that he was interested in. Cycling, cycling,” he said. “All the money he got for a birthday or something he would spend on socks or sunglasses. Nothing else interested him anymore.”

Pogačar has since emerged as the most dominant male rider of this century, and even Eddy Merckx has admitted the Slovenian could end up the best ever to race a bike.

The documentary traces his backstory and highlights a telling moment from one of Pogačar’s earliest races.

Hauptman, now a sports director at UAE Emirates-XRG, recalls arriving midway through a youth race in Ljubljana in 2012 and spotting a small rider apparently struggling several hundred meters behind the group.

“I came in the middle of the race, and one of our riders was really a few hundred meters behind the group. I spoke with the organizer, and said, ‘Why don’t we help this small guy to catch the group?’” Hauptman said. “He said, ‘Who? You mean this one? No, no, he will win. He overlapped the whole peloton.’”

“When you’re a kid, you just have fun. You don’t think too much about the future. I realized maybe the second year of juniors and U23 that I could go into the WorldTour and race the biggest races,” Pogačar said. “The first race I started, I finished last. I didn’t care. I just had such a good time.”

UAE signed him before he won the 2018 Tour de l’Avenir, and the trophies have been piling up ever since.

POG1 arrives a week after another documentary from Eurosport/TNT called Anatomy of a GOAT .

That film focused more on the physiology behind Pogačar’s success, revealing some interesting numbers on his heart rate, sleep scores, and heart rate variability from Whoop data.

Velo has seen only selected preview clips of the Colnago film, but it appears to focus more on his family, childhood, and personality, and traces the foundation of how Pogačar became the world No. 1.

Both documentaries come as the 28-year-old recovers from his devastating crash that ended his Vuelta a España and kept him out of the road worlds and Il Lombardia.

He’s already back to training and is set to reveal his 2027 racing calendar at UAE’s team camp in Spain next month.

items.title: 'The gap between second and first is humongous, and I've crossed that now' – Cameron Mason reflects on his breakthrough victory and that next piece of the puzzle
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
On Wednesday, Cameron Mason found what he'd been looking for over a number of years: victory in a major international cyclo-cross race. Raising his arms in Niel, the 26-year-old Scot became the first British rider since Tom Pidcock in 2022 to win a round of the Superprestige series.

Mason has racked up plenty of top-fives since graduating from the U23s to the elites in 2022-2023, along with the odd podium, but in the biggest series like the World Cup or Superprestige, victory has eluded him. Until now.

In muddy conditions that suited his technical prowess, the 777tv CX Team rider got rid of Michael Vanthourenhout and Joran Wyseure on the final lap to solo to a victory that will go down as a breakthrough moment.

But where does he go from here? And what doors might this victory now open?

caught up with Mason the day after the race to hear about his sense of relief and satisfaction, how he channeled his frustrations from the European Championships, and how he's trying to be a more complete rider than ever this season.

CN: You said after the race in Niel that it maybe hadn't sunk in yet. With a night to sleep on it, has it done so?

Yeah, when I spoke after the race, I had spent the last hour kind of just doing it. Since Euros, I was just wanting to do the ride I knew I could do, or knew I could have done on Sunday. Then there wasn't much more to say because I felt like I'd just shown exactly what I wanted to do. So that was a nice feeling of 'no excuses', and I didn't need to dress anything up. It was just exactly what you saw, which was an hour of being in control and being strong enough and smart enough to be first across the line.

And it still feels pretty fresh. I haven't really got a plan for what's next, which is fine. So I'm just enjoying it for what it is now. But there wasn't much of a big celebration because there's also that little bit of like... it's annoying that it was coming for so long. It wasn't a surprise, basically. There wasn't that shock or anything. It was more like 'finally', and like 'there you go' – showing everyone that's what I thought I could do years ago, and I've done it now. So that was a very satisfying feeling.

CN: Is there a bit of relief in there as well, or a sort of pressure lifted?

Yeah, there's a bit of relief. I think. I mean, I could have spent the next five years chasing that, and that would have been fine. Every year, I really enjoy the puzzle, and putting all the puzzle pieces together in pursuit of that next thing. The next thing happened to be winning a bike race, but three years ago, the next thing was getting on the podium, and before that, it was getting a professional contract. The goalposts just moved and so now, clearly the next thing is to win again, but that feels less daunting than it did.

The gap between getting second and first is humongous, it’s vast. Mentally and physically, the difference between being second best and being best is huge, and I've crossed that now. I'm not sure what I've learned yet, but I think when I turn up at the start line the next few races, I'll realise, 'OK, that's that's what changed'.

If I read that post, I still agree with it because I’ve had enough results to not be happy with some results, and that was a result I wasn't happy with. And it doesn't matter what other people say or how I got the result. It does get to a point where, if you keep getting a result despite an adversity it’s all well and good, but at the end of the day, I also just wanted a result where it was more simple. And Sunday wasn't really simple, you know. I messed up my start I had these massive gaps to bridge, and then I didn't play the final quite right, even for a medal after all of that.

I was probably being a bit… not optimistic, but I was kind of fantasising about the idea that ‘oh, on Sunday I maybe could have won’, which was probably still a bit ambitious, but I think just fantasising that meant that I could arrive on Wednesday, going, ‘right, well, maybe I can win this one’. No one will know if I could have won or not at Euros. But actually I can decide now. I can try and show everyone that I can win today. It was good timing.

CN: How are you feeling about this season in general? How has it been going and how good have you felt compared to previous seasons?

I feel about the same. At the start, it felt… not harder than ever, but like it felt as fast as ever. And the summer is very long. From my last race in February all the way to my first race again in October, there's a lot that goes on. You just spend all summer going ‘was that the right thing to do?’

The cyclo-cross season such a hard one to periodise because there's always a race, and they're all quite important, and it's just that constant revolving cast of guys on form, guys with problems, Thibau [Nys] coming in, Van der Poel maybe coming in later. It’s just constantly moving, and to pick a goal is really tricky.

What's similar to last year is that I didn't really decide to be this good at this moment. It just kind of happened. But when when that form comes, then you deal with it in a smart way. And I think we've done a really good job of that the last few weeks. We really aimed for Koppenbergcross, and that didn't quite work out physically but when you aim for something, you know that work is going to come through at some point, and it has done in the last couple weeks. And since Middelkerke, I've known that physically I'm there, technically I'm there, tactically there are things to work on, and then you just wait – well, for me it was just waiting until it rained a bit.

CN: The muddy stuff is where you feel you have a big advantage…?

It helps. Once the speeds come down a bit, and once every corner is a little bit more technical, then things just go a bit more in my favour. But the cool thing about this season has been I've been way more competitive on way more different types of courses. When I'm in good shape, it doesn't matter what the course is – if it's fast, if it's sandy or whatever – I’ll be there or thereabouts, but it means that when there's a course that really suits me, then then I've got that extra little edge.

But I'm trying to get away from the obsession with certain courses, because you might be sacrificing an opportunity on a course that you maybe wouldn't have thought you'd be that good at. Last year at the Euros it was a full sand course, bone dry, super fast, 30kph, but I was fighting for a medal. This year, I’m trying to think about it in a different way.

CN: Looking ahead, what what else would you like to get out of the season now?

I mean, there's loads of other races, so that's cool. I want to keep the consistency going. Yesterday was a bit of an outlier in my results – I've got quite a lot of fourths and fifths and sixths, and then I've got this one win – so just to be in in with a shot of winning again would be would be a like realistic goal, and hopefully I can keep this form for as long as I can.

CN: You hinted at it earlier, but is there anything you can tap into now in terms of that winning mindset? You hear of athletes in other sports that have that breakthrough win and something clicks and it sort of opens the floodgates.

Mentally, a bit of the pressure is off because I've proven to everyone and to myself that it's possible, and then yeah, I can turn that into confidence as well. Like, I know how to win, I've worked out how to win on this one specific race, parcours, day… then the puzzle is to do that on another day with different competition, different conditions, with different legs.

As I was saying, it's just another puzzle piece – now there's this piece of the puzzle that says I can win, so how do I do that again? It took like five years to do it, but how do I do it again? I was chatting to my coach this morning, and probably the best thing to do is do nothing. Just do exactly the same and carry on as if I didn't win. Logistically, the training, sleeping, eating, all that stuff needs to be just as good as it was for the last however many years. But the mindset thing, I feel more confident and that can't be a bad thing.

CN: What does the rest of the season hold in terms of your calendar?

need to work out if I'm going to do all the Superprestige races. That wasn't on my calendar, but now I'm leading the series overall, so I need to work out if I focus a bit more on that. I’m probably going to do all of the World Cups. Everyone's got the same puzzle. You can't do everything, so you’ve got to kind of pick and choose. I'll have a better idea after this weekend.

items.lbText:
Emotions are running high after the confirmation of Michael Carrick’s dismissal at Old Trafford. Here are some views from our readers

“A s a United fan who was around for the early 90s seeing Carrick go is a sad end to a horrible situation. He was the only likable thing about the club … I took my eight-year-old lad to Old Trafford for the Brighton game in the FA Cup in January and I’ve never experienced a more toxic atmosphere at a football ground. The fans deserve better … Better owners, better attitudes, better standards. Nothing will change with the setup of the club today and we are in this macabre holding pattern of failure, hope, anger and disappointment” – Chris

“Wilcox, [Berada] and [Jim] Ratcliffe should have fired themselves. They are the common denominator of all this failure. [Mauricio] Pochettino will last 12 months if he’s lucky” – Deb

“I have been a United supporter for over 60 years and this sacking just depresses me. Everyone knows the problem lies elsewhere … We were in desperate need of a left-back and centre-half. What did they do? Recruit several midfielders. So it starts again. Does anyone really believe changing manager will make any difference?” – Barry

“This feels sadder than every other time it’s happened since Alex Ferguson retired. Each of the previous managers had to go, as in large part the underperformance felt like it was their fault. This doesn’t feel like that … But, because the owners and executives aren’t going to sack themselves, and because you can’t fire the players, you change the only thing you can: the manager. And then repeat the cycle” – John

“I think it was Jonathan Liew who made the eminently sensible suggestion of a positional switch for Michael Carrick – by having him replace Jason Wilcox as director of football. That would have made sense” – Geoff

“Just waiting for Mr Mediocrity Wilcox to do the honourable thing and admit he is out of his depth and responsible in part for the situation and resign” – Andrew

“Since Fergie left there have been 12 managers at United, including interims, with little reward. Can all of these have been wrong? Surely they could not have been? It highlights the systemic failures of the club at all levels” – Simon

“Carrick remains a Manchester United legend, he will always be. Without corresponding changes in the club’s recruitment process and the people driving it, we will be back here after 12-18 months” – Wale

“There are many problems at United but the biggest is short-termism. Carrick, like Ole Gunnar Solskjær, was given the permanent job because he did a good job as caretaker, but those roles are very different. Building for the long term, even at a well-run club with solid foundations, is different from getting the best from the hand you’ve been dealt over a few months. Since Fergie retired managers have been sacked because results have taken a downturn, and those who’ve suggested things might need to get worse before they get better (Ralf Rangnick and Ruben Amorim) have been shown the door. There are no reasons to think it will be any different for Pochettino” – Jason

“Is Pochettino a good manager? He did well at Spurs – albeit without winning anything – and in a short spell at Southampton but that was a long time ago. Since then his record has been pretty underwhelming, up to and including an uninspiring time in charge of the US men’s team. He just seems to have a reputation as a good manager but I’m not really sure what it’s based on any more” – Jon

“The similarities between ENIC’s ownership of Tottenham and the Glazers stewardship of United are striking. It doesn’t bode well for United given Tottenham’s unprecedented two-and-a-half decades of underachievement since then. The main difference, further bad news for United, is that Tottenham’s perilous debt load primarily funded a new stadium rather than facilitating the owners’ stake in the company and subsequent dividends to themselves. Football clubs can’t withstand money being extracted – it all has to be re-invested to keep the wheels turning” – Paul

“In 53 years of supporting United this is the most depressing time. Worse, even, than the pre-Fergie years. The club is completely broken. The owners don’t really care about anything other than money. It’s a matter of public record that they see winning as nice to have [but] not the core objective of an elite football club … I feel deep sympathy for Carrick. His lack of experience was clear when appointed as interim. He did a great job and they rushed to appoint him permanently. It was predictable that the financial constraints of the club would mean he would fail and fail quickly. Our first team squad is completely below average quality and Carrick was completely undermined before the season started by an appallingly negligent transfer window. Every supporter knew where our problems would be and every one of us has been proved right. Why couldn’t Wilcox, Berrada et al see the same as us? It doesn’t matter who the manager is. With this squad and these owners the cycle will just continue” – Robert

“I have supported United for over 70 years through thick and thin but no more, to support United means supporting the Glazers. And I just wonder would a fans’ boycott get rid of them. An empty Old Trafford might do it” – Paul

“I am 62. I have followed Manchester United since the age of four (I found a picture of George Best, and told my mum I liked him). I stood on the Stretford End in my teens and took my son during the 90s. The fanbase needs to wrest control. The only way this will change is for the fanbase to boycott games. Stop going, stop providing matchday revenue. If the Glazers are only interested in the money, stop providing them with an income” – Bob…

items.title: The Antonelli you don't know: Inside the Mercedes garage with F1's new world champion
Fernandes rejects second Man Utd contract offer
items.content: <article>Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes rejects the club's second contract offer, with his current deal due to expire at the end of the season.</article>
items.lbText:
Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes has rejected a second contract offer from the club.

The Portugal midfielder is out of contract at the end of the season, though the club have the option to trigger a 12-month extension until 2028.

United are keen to avoid that eventuality by extending the 32-year-old's existing deal and have been in talks with the Portuguese's representatives in recent months.

But sources have told BBC Sport that Fernandes has rejected the club's second proposal over a new deal at Old Trafford.

Should United fail to agree a fresh deal with Fernandes, it is almost certain that the club will trigger a 12-month extension in his contract before 1 January.

How Ferguson-inspired Pochettino can succeed where Carrick failed at Man Utd

At that point, the midfielder would be able to sign a pre-contract agreement with foreign clubs as his contract would be within six months of expiring.

It is unclear when Fernandes turned down the offer, but it appears unlikely that a resolution is imminent given the upheaval at the club.

Michael Carrick was sacked as head coach on Thursday following the club's worst start to a domestic campaign in 40 years.

USA coach Mauricio Pochettino is expected to replace Carrick, with the Argentine set to be in charge for the first time when United travel to Anfield to face rivals Liverpool on 22 November.

United will be hoping that Pochettino's arrival will persuade Fernandes to commit his future to the club.

Fernandes came close to joining Pochettino's Tottenham in 2019 but a move failed to materialise, with the midfielder signing for United six months later.

The former Sporting midfielder has scored six times in 13 matches for United this season.

In theory, the current contract stand-off between Manchester United and Bruno Fernandes is not a big deal.

It is usual for the first, second and sometimes quite a few more offers to be rejected as part of the rough and tumble of negotiations.

United do have the option to trigger an option to add an extra year. However, there is reason why both sides might be wary to commit beyond that at this stage.

On Fernandes' part, there is a clear desire to compete for the biggest prizes. He can see the best years of his career drifting away. Yet again United have failed to build on a season of promise and he will now be wanting to see what impact Mauricio Pochettino has when he eventually arrives from the United States.

Fernandes was coveted by the Saudi Pro League 18 months ago, although the feeling has been he would prefer to stay in Europe.

On United's side, they will have noted Fernandes' alarming drop-off from the levels he hit last season, when he broke the Premier League assists record and won all the major player of the year honours.

Liverpool committed a huge amount of money to Mohamed Salah's last contract and that turned out to be a heavy financial burden. United will not want to get saddled with a major contract over an extended period for an underperforming player.

items.title: Which transfers worked in 2026, and which flopped? We analysed the data to find out the real impact of every move
items.author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
items.content:
Since UCI points have become so important for professional cycling teams, as the three-year totals determine which teams are eligible for the WorldTour, rider transfer have become an even more critical factor in teams' futures.

While the 2026-2027 transfers have yet to be fully completed, we can look back on which of the top acquisitions for the 2026 season have been the biggest successes and which teams suffered the most from not being able to hold onto top talent.

This year was the first of the three-year WorldTour promotion/relegation cycle, with the next relegation coming at the end of the 2028 season, and while the big-budget powerhouses like Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, UAE Team Emirates-XRG and Visma-Lease a Bike might be able to pour millions of euros into acquiring top riders, smaller teams have to be more strategic.

For teams like EF Education-EasyPost, Lotto-Intermarché, NSN and Groupama-FDJ, who were at the bottom quarter of the UCI Team Rankings, their recruitment strategy will be critical for remaining in the WorldTour as upstart ProTeams climb ahead in search of WorldTour promotion in 2029.

Teams have to be in the top 18 of the rankings, calculated by adding the points scored by each team's top 20 riders, to qualify for the WorldTour.

While it's still early days, Pinarello-Q36.5 made enormous strides toward qualifying for the WorldTour, thanks to their top rider Tom Pidcock, but also through smart signings like Quinten Hermans from Alpecin, Aimé De Gendt from Cofidis, Fred Wright from Bahrain Victorious and Chris Harper from Jayco-AlUla.

Pinarello-Q36.5 finished the season as the 12th best team and the top ProTeam of the year, with Tudor next best in 16th place. Both teams will earn automatic invitations to all of the WorldTour races including the Tour de France next year, which will help them earn even more points toward qualifying for the 2029-2031 WorldTour.

On the other side of the equation, Picnic-PostNL had an extremely worrying season. The team lost Tobias Lund Andresen, who went on to have a brilliant year for Decathlon CMA CGM, as well as GC hopeful Oscar Onley, who went to Netcompany Ineos.

Not only did Picnic-PostNl finish dead last of the WorldTour teams in the rankings, they landed in 30th of all teams - on the cusp of not even qualifying for a Grand Tour invitation if they didn't have a WorldTour license that gives them an automatic entry.

If Picnic-PostNL survive the allegations of a toxic culture and continue on toward 2029, the men's team faces a very difficult battle to climb out of the relegation zone since they are already almost 7,000 points behind 18th-placed Cofidis.

Also on the concerning side were Groupama-FDJ, who ended the year in 20th, although not so far behind 18th as to panic just yet.

*The graphics below are all interactive, so you can hover over the bars for more information and in some cases, change the filter to only show transfers.

The Belgian had a banner season, winning the time trial titles at the UCI Road World Championships and European Championships, won two stages of the Tour de France and came second overall, won the Amstel Gold Race, GP de Québec and his fifth Clásica San Sebastián.

Evenepoel benefited greatly from a strong support crew in the Tour de France, where Jai Hindley, Maxim Van Gils, fellow Soudal departure Mattia Cattaneo, and Jan Tratnik were his main support in the mountains.

While he still couldn't match Tadej Pogačar, he did hold off the Slovenian's right-hand man Isaac del Toro to go one place better than his previous best with Soudal-Quickstep in the GC. Evenepoel scored a massive 7,191.61 points this year, with fractions coming from team time trials, and this was the most scored of any of the riders who transfered to new teams in 2026.

The second best rider was Benoit Cosnefroy, who left Decathlon for UAE Team Emirates-XRG. Cosnefroy had a solid year of shorter stage races and one-day classics, taking wins in the Coppa Sabatini and GP du Morbihan, the overall Boucles de la Mayenne, third in Amstel and fourth in La Flèche Wallonne. He didn't race any Grand Tours, but still raked in 2,355.28 points for his team.

Next up in the list was Tobias Lund Andresen who left Picnic-PostNL to join Decathlon, making the most of the switch to win the Cadel Evans Great Ocean Road Race, a stage of the Tour Down Under and Tirreno-Adriatico, and podiums in In Flanders Field and the Copenhagen Sprint. His season might have been an even greater success had he not stopped in June after contracting the Epstein-Barr virus.

Jasper Stuyven's departure from Lidl-Trek for Soudal-Quickstep seemed to rejuvenate the 34-year-old, who claimed the podium in Paris-Roubaix - his best result in a major classic since his 2021 Milan-San Remo win. He also finished in the top 10 in San Remo, the Tour of Flanders, and three stages of the Giro, then capped the year off with second in Paris-Tours for a total of 1,903.88 points.

Of the neo-pros, Jarno Widar (Lotto-Intermarché) topped the list of incoming riders, ending the season with a bang with second behind Pogačar on stage 4 of the Vuelta and two other stage top 10s, then went on to win Tre Valli Varesine and a stage and the overall in the Tour of Guangxi to take in 1,302 points - the second highest tally of his team.

Jakob Omrzel (Bahrain Victorious) wasn't far behind, with seventh overall in the Vuelta and a spectacular stage win at Calar Alto from the breakaway. With a podium in the Tour of Slovenia and a top 10 overall in the Tour of the Alps, Omrzel ended the year with 1,046 points.

A fresh start helped Evenepoel, Cosnefroy and Stuyven in the list of most improved after transferring, with Evenepoel netting 3,064 more points this year than he did in 2025.

Cosnefroy improved by 1,970 after a 2025 season hampered by a knee injury. Slotting into the mix was Anthon Charmig, who moved from XDS Astana to Uno-X Mobility.

Charmig's move to a more familiar team culture may have been a factor behind his great season, with top 10s in the Tour Down Under GC, a stage win in the Tour Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes and podiums in five late-season one-day races including the GP de Québec.

After scoring just a few hundred points with Astana, Charmig ended the year with a massive 1,396 points this year and was ranked 49th in the world. It was a fantastic season for the Dane.

Which teams won the prize for best hirings? It depends a bit on how you measure the success. In terms of net total points - adding points by new arrivals minus the 2026 points scored by riders who left - Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe gained the most, largely thanks to Evenepoel, with 8,188 points.

Netcompany Ineos got great results from new hires Dorian Godon - winner of stages in Paris-Nice, Tour de Romandie and Volta a Catalunya - and Oscar Onley, who was sixth overall in the Vuelta a España among other fine results.

Pinarello-Q36.5's tally was the third highest, showing that the ambitious Swiss team are well on their way to qualifying for the WorldTour in 2029. Quinten Hermans steadily picked up points all year, with top finishes in the Renewi Tour and De Brabantse Pijl his most valuable contributions.

While Decathlon CMA CGM earned 6,217 from new arrivals like Tobias Lund Andresen from Picnic-PostNL, sprinter Olav Kooij from Visma, and Riccitello from Israel-Premier Tech, they actually lost out, because their gains did not completely offset their losses of Cosnefroy to UAE and Dorian Godon to Netcompany Ineos.

If we look at the percentage of points gained by incoming riders and ignore the total points, NSN Cycling tops the list. After changing their identity from Israel-Premier Tech, NSN Cycling earned almost 41% of their total points from incoming riders such as Biniam Girmay, Lewis Askey and Alessandro Pinarello.

Even though they ended the season with a net positive transfer score after losing Derek Gee-West to Lidl-Trek and Matthew Riccitello to Decathlon, their returning riders like Corbin Strong and Marco Frigo had relatively lacklustre seasons and the team actually fell five places in the UCI Team Rankings.

Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe had 37% of their total come from incoming riders, mainly Evenepoel but also solid results from neo-pro Luke Tuckwell - second overall in the Tour Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes and leader for two stages, and Gianni Vermeersch who had a solid Classics campaign after leaving Alpecin, with fifth in Strade Bianche his most notable result.

Drilling down to perhaps the most important factor in the UCI Team Rankings is the team's position and whether it improved or fell with the team's new composition in 2026. The above graph charts the percentage of points scored by incoming riders, the team's change in rank relative to 2025 and the total points scored by new arrivals.

Pinarello-Q36.5 both had a large portion of their points come from transfers and the biggest gain in position, gaining seven places and rocketing into the top 18 at 12th.

The merger between Lotto and Intermarché was the main factor behind their rise in the rankings from 23rd and 24th for the two parent teams to 16th. Jarno Widar, who graduated from Lotto's devo team, was the top earner with his victories in Guangxi and Tre Valli Varesine.

Decathlon CMA CGM ended the year with a gain of three spots in the UCI Team Rankings thanks in large part to their young phenom Paul Seixas and reliable GC man Felix Gall, even if their net transfer value was in the negative territory.

Soudal-Quickstep, but losing Evenepoel, slid five positions to tenth place, and while they have to rebuild from here, they're not in much danger of relegation.

The same can't be said for Picnic-PostNL. This graph really emphasises their terrible year - they dropped a massive 13 spots and had very few points from incoming riders, showing no positive direction in any of the measures. They only won three races all year, and only a single WorldTour stage by Frits Biesterbos in the Tour of Guangxi.

The net total of a team's transfer strategy doesn't tell the whole story, however, because one big signing like Evenepoel can overshadow a wider roster shift that can bode well for the future. Even the average points can fall victim to the same problem of outliers.

The median score can be a better measure, unless there were very few new riders in a team.

Bahrain Victorious seem to have done well in most measures: they had a net gain of almost 2,300 points, a gain of three positions in the UCI Team Rankings going from 10th to seventh, and the highest median points per new rider.

That included performances by Giro d'Italia stage winner Alec Segaert, neo-pro Jakob Omrzel, who won a stage and finished seventh overall in the Vuelta a España, and consistent seasons from Pau Miquel and Alessandro Borgo.

Lidl-Trek, while not getting the most out of Juan Ayuso, still earned over 1,700 points from the Spaniard and almost 1,300 from Derek Gee-West, and good value from Max Walscheid and Matteo Sobrero for the second highest median score.

Once again, Picnic-PostNL are dead last, showing that their new hires just aren't paying off, with the exception of Biesterbos.

Looking at the points scored by riders leaving a team tells an interesting story. Soudal-Quickstep of course, with Evenepoel's departure, bled out in 2026 gaining only 3,806 points from incoming riders but seeing departing riders score over 8,000 points between Evenepoel and Luke Lamperti's haul for EF Education-EasyPost.

However, between Paul Magnier and Tim Merlier, the team softened the blow, holding onto the top 10 in the team rankings.

Lotto-Intermarché suffered by losing Girmay, winner of the Clásica Almeria, a stage of the Belgium Tour and third in the Tour de France points classification with five top-10 finishes in stages. Their story is complicated by the fact that Lotto and Intermarché merged before 2026, so their departing riders' total is inflated as half the team left.

But Picnic-PostNL's total is not. They lost Lund, Onley and Kevin Vermaerke and only picked up a significant number of points from bringing Biesterbos in from the BEAT Continental team. The 24-year-old was their second-top scorer behind Pavel Bittner, who is leaving for Pinarello-Q36.5 in 2027.

There were also a few transfers that didn't quite work out as expected - with Juan Ayuso most notably struggling to match his 2025 performance with UAE Team Emirates and ending up with almost 900 fewer points than last year, but it could have been much higher had it not been for bad luck.

Oscar Onley and Kévin Vauquelin's totals were even more significantly lower at 1,545 and 1,409 less, respectively.

Onley traded a fourth place overall in the Tour de France last year for sixth place overall after an early crash and illness in the Vuelta. He missed the Tour because he injured his shoulder in a crash in the Tour Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes. Vauquelin finished fourth in Paris-Nice but had an unremarkable Tour de France.

Fred Wright took a while to get going after switching from Bahrain Victorious to Pinarello-Q36.5 after suffering a bizarre infection due to a thorn getting stuck in his knee during a training camp in Chile but ended the season with some solid one-day race results including the British road title.

: A thorough look at the 2025-2026 UCI Women's WorldTour and ProTeams and an analysis of the 2026-2027 transfer market.

items.title: ‘My Peak Level Must Become My Base’: Evenepoel Lays Out His Plan to Beat Pogačar
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: VIDEO: Evenepoel reveals his new training framework and sketches out his strategy for the ‘anti-Pogačar’ 2027 Tour de France in Specialized feature.
items.lbText:
(Photo: Maximilian Fries / Red Bull Content Pool)

Remco Evenepoel puts it all out there in a new long-form video interview with Specialized.

After a blockbuster first year with Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, the Belgian star rates his season (“eight out of 10”), shares his take on the 2027 Tour de France route (he digs it), and offers intriguing insights into how his training has changed.

Released Thursday, the “Remco Evenepoel: Pursuit of Perfect” YouTube show is the latest in a flurry of off-season “rider does content” releases.

Tadej Pogačar got the red carpet treatment in not one, but two, feature documentaries , and Sepp Kuss broke YouTube with his “day in the life” video.

As a Specialized production, the conversation leans heavily on the rider’s “love” of his Tarmac and Shiv, and how he’s refining his position for 2027.

However, Evenepoel also speaks for the first time on the hottest topic of the past month: the 2027 Tour de France route.

The course for next year’s Tour de France has been labeled “anti-Pogačar” and “pro-Remco.”

Evenepoel is, of course, delighted with a parcours that offers the most time trialing in 15 years.

The four-time TT world champion can build a buffer in 71km against the clock that will buy him breathing room in the mountains.

“I’m very happy. If you see the most amount of TTs since 2012, that’s pretty good,” Evenepoel says in the video. “I would love it [the TTs] to be even a bit longer, but I’m very happy with what we’ve got.”

Evenepoel finished a distant second to Pogačar at the 2026 Tour de France.

However, next year offers him a slim chance to go one step better.

Evenepoel tells podcast host Ben Edwards that he and his entourage will spend winter figuring out how he can maximize his strengths for next summer’s showdown with Pog.

“I need to be able to bring my one-day TT performance into the grand tours,” Evenepoel says.

“In the world championships, I put a minute into [Filippo] Ganna, and at the Chrono des Nations, I put two minutes into [Jay] Vine. If I can bring those performances into the grand tours, I’d gain even more.

“What is now my ‘very good’ must now become the standard,” he continues. “Over winter we’ll have to see how and when, and why we can or can’t do that. I’m sure with all the knowledge the team and my little crew around me have, and with my own experience, that we can find that.”

Evenepoel adds that he hopes to devise an energy management plan so that he can peak for his key stages of the Tour and play defense elsewhere.

“We need to make a strategy to come into those TTs fresh and really use them to see what time they will bring,” he says.

Maybe Evenepoel’s new training framework will help.

In the video, the 26-year-old discusses how Tim Heemskerk – the former coach of Jonas Vingegaard – revolutionized his approach to training.

The Dutch staffer joined Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe mid-season and brought a new data-driven approach to workouts.

“Tim really wanted all sorts of inside information – sleeping metrics, weight, HRV, all that stuff. He wanted it every single day,” Evenepoel says.

“He wanted it first thing in the morning so he could see how the values were overnight. Then he could adapt something [for the coming workout] if necessary,” Evenepoel says. “That was never a way I’ve been thinking.”

The video runs to almost an hour in length, but it’s well worth a watch. What else are you going to do now there’s no road racing to binge on?

Watch the full show on Specialized’s YouTube channel.

items.title: Ferrari's Leclerc-Hamilton problem is far from solved
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Don't be fooled by Ferrari's Formula 1 drivers playing nicely in Brazil; there are still very real tensions between Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton.

The drivers and team principal Fred Vasseur got together in Brazil to try to talk things through after Hamilton's extraordinary criticism of Leclerc following their victory-losing Mexico run-in.

That meeting proved constructive, and Leclerc and Hamilton were very well-behaved during the Brazilian Grand Prix, even following team orders and leaving each other plenty of room, unlike in Mexico.

Hamilton's summary was: "Everything's good. Fred brought us together. Fred was great in the meeting. And then he just left me and Charles to just give our points.

"We both had a really good, open discussion. And it's all good now. We'll just move on."

But you can't compare Mexico and Brazil, so Vasseur didn't bother reaching for what would have been an easy pat-on-the-back.

"You can't compare the two situations," Vasseur said, in respect of Leclerc and Hamilton's cordiality on-track at Interlagos.

"Honestly, we had a good discussion on Friday. We cleared the situation. We did a good reset on the mindset.

"They left my room joking together. It's good. I hope that it will last, to stay like this."

All Vasseur can do for now is "hope" it lasts because that Brazil fight was only ever going to be for minor points-paying positions, not a race win or a podium.

So there's every reason to believe that when the Ferrari is back fighting for wins, be it in Las Vegas or Qatar or Abu Dhabi, Hamilton and Leclerc are going to be back fighting tooth and nail.

After all, Leclerc admitted post-meeting: "Of course there is tension, of course we want to finish ahead of each other, and sometimes we are not going to do things right, and it's OK sometimes to disagree on the way you see things.

"But at the same time discussing about those helps a whole lot."

In light of the Leclerc-Hamilton tensions, Leclerc's ex-team-mate at Ferrari Carlos Sainz was asked about his time with Leclerc.

Hamilton had, after all, pointed to Leclerc's time alongside Sainz and Sebastian Vettel as evidence that he races his team-mates harder.

"I have relatively good memories of my time with Charles and the fights we had," Sainz said in Brazil.

"It is true that when you're fighting for wins, there's always more pressure, more things down the line. So you become naturally a bit more selfish than when you are fighting in the midfield for a P8 or a P9.

"It's more difficult maybe to follow exactly the ideal situation that the team would like you to follow, because there's a win down the line. There was wins down the line back then, but I always respected Charles. He always respected me. We never had contacts or anything like this. We just had strong fights. You remember Monza, Vegas. There was plenty of hot moments during the year.

"What was difficult more was the fanbase. The PR and the fanbase was really ignited back then, and it was very polarised between Charles and me. And I remember suffering a bit from the very hardcore fans of Charles insulting or wishing me bad.

"Maybe some Italian media also saying that I was not being enough of a number two when I needed to be, and vice-versa whenever Charles had to do it.

"So it's more the pressure surrounding Ferrari, that involves Ferrari, than the actual issues that I had with Charles, which were always resolved that same night when we called each other with a more cold head and we always managed to find the solution and the way forward."

Sainz felt it is an inevitable problem with having two equals in the same team.

"I cannot remember no Formula 1 team that has had two good drivers fighting at the front that haven't had issues when fighting for wins," Sainz added.

"You can choose whether to have a number two as a second driver, or you can have two good drivers that will create those issues. But you cannot have one without the other, in my opinion. And you will never have one without the other.

"Maybe in Ferrari it gets a bit exacerbated with everything that involves Ferrari, but I cannot remember a moment where this hasn't happened. It happened in Mercedes. It happened in McLaren the last few years. It happened in Ferrari.

"So I don’t know when it hasn't happened. It is part of Formula 1. And if you are a team principal and you know you're going to have two great drivers, you're always going to have that issue.

"I don't think you can ever calm those two guys 100% down and expect them not to go for a move for a race win."

Why Leclerc-Hamilton is different

There are some parallels to the tensions in 2019 when Leclerc managed to steal Ferrari away from four-time world champion Sebastian Vettel as a 21-year-old. This piece by Mark Hughes still stands as an excellent account of that.

Back then, the drivers were 'free to race', the team principal (Mattia Binotto) tried to play things fairly, the drivers were close enough in performance to routinely be near each other on track, and there was a huge battle for supremacy.

Leclerc ultimately won that battle convincingly, with Sainz brought into replace Vettel, but never as an equal to Leclerc. (That didn't mean he was a dutiful number two either. He was too quick for that.)

Leclerc and Sainz had their flashpoints, but ultimately things never uncontrollably spilt over for one good reason: Leclerc was ahead of Sainz around two-thirds of the time.

The dynamic therefore was very different: Leclerc even ended up helping Sainz to the only non-Verstappen victory of 2023 in Singapore. That was evidence of Leclerc playing the long game, knowing a small sacrifice there would only strengthen his position once Ferrari had a title-challenging car.

There was ultimately enough of a performance gap for there never to be too much needle between them. Leclerc didn't see Sainz as a threat to his position as Ferrari's spearhead. He was right, as Ferrari chose to replace Sainz with Hamilton just a few months after that Singapore win.

And it's no coincidence that in 2025, there being a clear performance gap between Leclerc and Hamilton meant there wasn't much needle between them.

Suddenly they're very closely matched in 2026, and the Leclerc-Vettel era tension is immediately re-exposed because now there is a threat to Leclerc's position. Leclerc was previously fairly comfortable, like Vettel was in 2015-18 as the focal point of the team, with team-mate Kimi Raikkonen very much a support act.

Now there is an active battle for supremacy. If Ferrari improves its power unit and has a title-challenging car next year, both Hamilton and Leclerc want to be the one leading that charge.

It's why the prospect of Ferrari's Brazil meeting being any kind of full stop on its Leclerc-Hamilton problem is absolute nonsense.

That's not going to change until Leclerc has destroyed another world champion - as he did to Vettel - or until he's the one destroyed by a team-mate.

items.title: Pochettino’s Chelsea maelstrom the best yardstick for what lies ahead at United
items.author: Andrew Beasley
items.content:
Argentinian oversaw high-scoring games in his one Chelsea season and Opta predicts his Manchester United side will move upfield quicker than that team

Among the 20 managers with more than 290 matches in the Premier League, only the five “big beasts” of Alex Ferguson, Arsène Wenger, José Mourinho, Jürgen Klopp and Pep Guardiola have better points-per-game averages than Mauricio Pochettino. He is an elite manager.

Pochettino took over Southampton midway through their first season back in the top flight (2012-13) after the club spent seven years in the lower leagues. In his only full campaign, they finished eighth. He led Tottenham to second in 2016-17, third in the seasons either side, and reached the 2019 Champions League final. His presence lifted those clubs.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
Argentinian oversaw high-scoring games in his one Chelsea season and Opta predicts his Manchester United side will move upfield quicker than that team

A mong the 20 managers with more than 290 matches in the Premier League, only the five “ big beasts ” of Alex Ferguson, Arsène Wenger, José Mourinho, Jürgen Klopp and Pep Guardiola have better points-per-game averages than Mauricio Pochettino. He is an elite manager.

Pochettino took over Southampton midway through their first season back in the top flight (2012-13) after the club spent seven years in the lower leagues. In his only full campaign, they finished eighth. He led Tottenham to second in 2016-17, third in the seasons either side, and reached the 2019 Champions League final . His presence lifted those clubs.

However, the Argentinian has competed in only one of the past six Premier League campaigns. Winning Ligue 1 and the Coupe de France in an 18-month spell with Paris Saint-Germain tells us little. His most pertinent recent experience for the Manchester United job is the 2023-24 season he spent at Chelsea, a campaign that left more questions than answers.

The club had finished 12th the season before, in the first year of the Todd Boehly/Clearlake Capital era. Pochettino was always likely to take Chelsea higher. And he did. But his influence is harder to judge. Opta predicted Chelsea would finish sixth in 2023-24, a forecast that proved correct. By this measure Pochettino hit par though, as Transfermarkt rated the market value of his squad as the third-highest in the Premier League in October 2023, perhaps he fell short.

The squad value grew thanks to remarkable investment. Chelsea spent more than any other club in Europe’s big five leagues in each of the three transfer windows from the summer of 2022 to the summer of 2023. Working for Boehly will have provided a good primer for the madness of Manchester United, even if the spending won’t be as generous.

Assembling a winning team from a rapidly evolving squad is not easy. Pochettino crafted a side that delivered the fifth-most expected points in 2023-24. Chelsea’s 63.4 was a fair way shy of Arsenal (81.2), Manchester City (79.3) and Liverpool (76.2) but it was a decent first season.

Chelsea conceded 63 league goals, the club’s worst figure in the Premier League era. Yet only twice have they amassed more than the 77 goals they scored. They were a little above their expected goal figures at each end but the bulk of their large goal totals was reflected in the underlying data.

But even the xG numbers raised questions, because Chelsea benefited from 12 penalties, the joint-second-most in the past 10 Premier League seasons. Chelsea have had 14 in their 86 league games since Pochettino left. They conceded five penalties and committed the joint-most Opta-defined defensive errors leading to shots (22) in Pochettino’s season.

Across three matches in April 2024 they drew 2-2 with the bottom side Sheffield United, thumped Everton 6-0 then lost 5-0 at Arsenal. They endured a similar seesaw sequence earlier in the campaign, losing 4-1 at Tottenham and Newcastle, with a 4-4 draw against Manchester City in between. Chelsea also set the record for matches in which a team score and concede at least two goals in a 38-game Premier League season (12). How do you assess a manager’s performance in that maelstrom?

If the low point was not the Arsenal loss, it was being called “ billion-pound bottle jobs ” by Gary Neville after losing the 2024 Carabao Cup final. Never mind that Chelsea had enough chances to win, Pochettino had to answer for the defeat. Less than three months later, he was gone.

The Premier League has evolved in Pochettino’s relatively brief absence. Arne Slot arrived, won the title and left, while Guardiola’s departure leaves no big managerial beasts remaining. There have been tactical shifts, with increased man-to-man marking across the pitch, and set-piece skirmishes have decided more matches than feels healthy.

Opta’s data shows Pochettino’s probable new side move upfield more quickly but press less intensely than his Chelsea team. There will need to be an adjustment. But can a manager whose training methods at Chelsea were described by a well-placed source as “antiquated” get up to speed as quickly as United need?

Pochettino will adapt and his Premier League record commands the utmost respect. The relevance of his recent work to United in 2026-27 is less clear.

items.title: Whatever happened to the diamond that went missing in F1 crash?
items.content: <article>Whatever happened to the diamond that went missing after the Formula 1 car it was attached to crashed?</article>
items.lbText:
Where were you between the hours of 1pm and 3pm on 23 May 2004?

If you were in Monaco, consider yourself a suspect - or at least a witness - in Formula 1's biggest unsolved mystery.

A $300,000 diamond was last seen stuck to the front of an F1 car before it crashed on the first lap of the Grand Prix and it still has not been found 22 years later.

Did someone pick it up? Was it swept up with all the debris? Did it slip down a drain? Was it even a real diamond?

The reason why a 1.4 carat diamond was attached to the most delicate part of a car that reaches 200mph in a race was straightforward: publicity.

Jaguar Racing's results on the track had been mediocre at best since becoming an F1 team in 2000 and by 2004 its parent company Ford had decided it would be pulling them out of the sport.

"My job flipped from primarily running the team to primarily selling the team and finding a new owner or they would shut it down," former team principal Tony Purnell tells BBC Sport.

"It was probably the worst year of my life. Particularly because for the first few months I was sworn to secrecy."

His team needed some good PR to divert attention away from performance and improve its appeal.

They had enjoyed a successful promotional weekend in Silverstone the previous season thanks to a tie-up with Terminator 3 and so director of communications Nav Sidhu was looking to recreate the magic with another bit of help from a movie.

"I'd heard on the grapevine, around about the winter of 2003, that they were making Ocean's Twelve and we discovered that they were shooting some of the scenes in Monte Carlo," Sidhu says.

"One thing led to another and before you knew it, we had agreed [a deal] with George Clooney, Brad Pitt and Matt Damon."

Sidhu had arranged with legendary Hollywood producer Jerry Weintraub to have the film's branding and stars take over the team for the Monaco weekend.

The film plot centred on an audacious theft of a diamond-encrusted Faberge egg. Sidhu decided he wanted some sparkle on his cars too at the most glamorous race in the F1 calendar.

Sidhu negotiated with diamond company Steinmetz that the two Jaguar cars would have gems - which would today be worth about $1m in total - attached to them.

What happened next, though, was not part of the script.

While the champagne corks were popping on nearby mega yachts in the principality, the diamonds were being hand-delivered into the garages. There were two that would be mounted on to the car and a larger gem just for the photos.

The diamonds for the cars were encased by steel and fixed to the nose cones. One on experienced driver Mark Webber's car and one on rookie Christian Klien's.

Webber was starting from 11th place in the grid and Klien - in only his sixth race - was starting from 14th. They weren't expected to challenge for the podium, but they were expected to bring the diamonds back.

Monaco's street circuit is demanding, with narrow roads, tight turns and a tunnel.

Overtaking is difficult and crashes are common - as Klien soon found out.

In a chaotic first lap, the Austrian made contact with one of the Jordan cars exiting the Mirabeau corner. This damaged the front of his car - where the diamond was - and led to a slow collision with the barriers at the famous Loews hairpin.

Klien climbed out unhurt but the front of the car was crumpled.

It was not long before Sidhu had the diamond company on the phone asking if they would get their diamond back.

"I can't remember what I answered, but it certainly wasn't 'yes'," he says.

He couldn't even get on to the track to have a look as the race had another 76 laps to go and only then would the car - which had been lifted off the track by a crane and left behind the barriers - return to the garage.

"I was consumed with getting to that spot as quickly as I possibly could," Sidhu says.

"That hour and a half waiting for the race to finish felt like a day and a half, every single lap was just like pulling teeth."

By the time he had the chance to have a look, there was no sign of the diamond.

Sidhu completely denies the rumours of a fake diamond.

"I've learned that any diamond company is not going to go out there, particularly in the public domain, and use fake diamonds because clearly there's a high risk of being caught," he says.

"Had we used a fake diamond in that car and what took place took place, then clearly the embarrassment and the disrepute it would bring Jaguar, and Formula 1 for that matter, was too high risk.

"There's been loads of conspiracy theories about was it a real diamond or was Christian told to crash his car and I think that's what's given the story its life - there's a mystery to this story and that mystery will always breed different theories."

Purnell backs up the legitimacy of the diamond, recalling a conversation he had with the managing director of the team, David Pitchforth.

"David said, 'Tony, it was definitely real because when they came to the office with it, I picked the diamond up, went to the window and scratched the window' because that's how to tell.

"Hearing that from Dave, I'm in no doubt it was the real thing that was put on the car.

"I don't know if one of our mechanics was switched on enough to make a fake, but I don't think so."

"I think somebody probably just picked it up, put it in their pocket and... they're probably smiling and thinking, 'it's in my drawer'," says Purnell.

"I do think also that a fairly large diamond zooming through at 100 miles an hour probably shattered. Somebody's got a little bit, somebody else has got another [little bit].

"Maybe, sadly, just some guy was sweeping up the road or one of those trucks with the brushes and it all went down the sewer.

"It did occur to me that the ultimate thing would be if Clooney, Pitt and Damon had contrived to steal it because it was so in line with Ocean's Eleven. But that was a fantasy too far."…

items.title: Yankees news: Corey Seager in trade rumors
items.author: Kento Mizuno
items.content:
MLB Trade Rumors | Darragh McDonald: The Yankees are seeking upgrades in several spots this offseason, and McDonald provides a useful overview of the latest rumblings of what they might do. Perhaps the most eye-catching name mentioned is Corey Seager, who Jon Heyman claims that the Yankees have talked to the Rangers about. Color me skeptical for a variety of reasons: Seager has full no-trade protection, and as an oft-injured middle infielder on the wrong side of 30, I’m not sure he’s worth taking on the remainder of his contract, or shelling out prospect capital to get the Rangers to eat some of it. Elsewhere, the Yankees have been connected to Luis Arraez and Brandon Lowe at second base, and Carson Kelly at catcher. Of course, the CBA negotiations cast a pall of uncertainty over everything, and it’s possible that the Yankees will stay put until a deal is within sight.

NJ.com | Randy Miller: The narrative around how Anthony Volpe turned his season around following his second minor-league stint in 2026 is a bit overblown – he had a 95 wRC+ from September 10 onwards, which is above his career average but still nothing to write home about – but it was nice to see him hit for a respectable average and regain his mojo defensively over the stretch run. Apparently, a talk with Scott Boras might have been the catalyst for Volpe’s bounceback. Volpe reportedly reached out to Boras sometime this year to collect feedback about his game. Although it’s not clear what advice was given, there’s reason to believe Boras knows what he’s talking about; before he became the game’s premier agent, Boras was a second baseman in the St. Louis Cardinals’ system. Evidently, Volpe must have appreciated the feedback, as he dropped his former agency, WME Sports, to sign with Boras Corp. just before the playoffs. One can only hope that Boras’ Volpe-whispering powers will lead to an even better 2027 campaign from the embattled infielder.

MLB.com | Jim Callis: Finally, another story from the AFL; after stalling as a catching prospect, 24-year-old Antonio Gomez is now trying to make it as a flamethrowing reliever. The Yankees signed Gomez out of Venezuela in 2018 based on his arm strength, but while his defense progressed throughout the minors, his bat couldn’t keep up. In 2025, the Yankees approached him about giving pitching a chance, and while the results haven’t quite been there yet, the raw stuff is impressive – triple digits on his heater, with a mid-90s cutter, an upper-90s sinker, and a mid-80s slider. I have a soft spot for prospects with unusual development paths, so I’ll be rooting for Gomez to harness his stuff.

items.title: Game Preview: Knicks at Pacers, November 13, 2026
items.author: Moritz Wollert
items.content:
There are sports movies, there are even some good sports movies. And then there is .

As a basketball romantic you are definitely not flipping the channel when old ball coach Norman Dale a.k.a. Gene Hackman drives his 1951 Chevy Styleline Deluxe through the backwoods of Indiana all the way to the little town of Hickory, where he hopes to find a new life, new love and redemption. You let yourself be mesmerized by Angelo Pizzo’s and David Anspaugh’s timeless fairytale, by the very essence of “Hoosier Hysteria,” the beautiful yet tragic tribulations of high school sports, the rough, simple charm of small town America. And you enjoy every second of it, despite a rather predictable underdog story unfolding in front of your eyes that Hollywood has repeated many times over.

The current Indiana Pacers would kill for some of that predictability, the kind they expected going into this season. After a surprising Finals berth in 2025, their following year was doomed by Tyrese Haliburton’s ruptured Achilles. They punted on the next campaign and thought, with their point guard’s return, everything would return normal; that the half-court offense would run smooth as a “picket fence;” and that the jumpers would automatically fall like the ones by Jimmy Chitwood. But Haliburton (unfortunately) isn’t as quiet nor as down to earth as Mr. Chitwood, nor is an NBA season comparable to a Hollywood movie. It’s a lot more complicated than that.

The Pacers are finding that out the hard way. It only took testy Tyrese a handful of games until he got injured again (it’s a hamstring now) and his team sorely misses the All Star as their 4-8 record puts them in the lower region of the Eastern Conference. On Friday against the New York Knicks, Haliburton will also be reduced to trolling from the sidelines, and he won’t be able to right the wrongs that have plagued his squad so far this season. It’s a huge advantage for Mike Brown’s men as Haliburton is the straw that stirs the Apple Cider for Indiana. Most of their strategy revolves around his talent, his scoring and his distribution.

But it’s not like the Pacers are just struggling out of the gate because Hali has only played four games. Even with him they lost to Milwaukee, barely got by New Orleans and were annihilated by Dallas. Indiana can’t shoot threes (just over 33 percent), despite a traditionally fast pace their offense isn’t even close to functioning well (20th in offensive rating), and their D is nothing to write home about either (15th in the league). The Pacers are an atrocious rebounding team (29th in rebounding percentage) and they struggle mightily to hit their free throws.

Do they do anything well? They do, in fact, take good care of the ball and have a one of the best assist-to-turnover-ratios in the entire Association. Individually Pascal Siakam is enjoying a strong start to the season (22.7 points) and Andrew Nembhard has come firing out of the gates as well (17.1 points, 42.9 percent from downtown). A lot of guys are still left from that Finals team two years ago, so in theory they should know what it takes. And Rick Carlisle is still a tremendously respected coach, at least when he isn’t whining like a five year old who didn’t get his wish at Toys-R-Us.

The skipper really has his work cut out for him early in the year. New center Ivica Zubac, a classic, plodding back-to-basket big man with considerable post skills, hasn’t really found his place in an adjusted Pacers system that once was predicated on playing five-out at all costs. Continuity has also been a big issue as Carlisle has already started 11 different players, at times making it seem like the Pacers are still on their tanking ways from last year. They obviously aren’t and it should be noted that slow starts are nothing new for Indiana under Carlisle. Consider yourself warned.

With Friday’s game being another Cup contest you can bet that the Pacers will be highly motivated and our beloved Knicks better be ready for a hostile environment. Keep calm if Haliburton tries some stupid sideline voodoo as he certainly will when he senses a camera being on him. Feed Karl-Anthony Towns in a favorable matchup for him, let Brunson do his thing against Indiana’s supposed Brunson stoppers who always seem to just limit him to 35. Make use of your more talented depth, outshoot the struggling shooting team and control the tempo. Just show that you are the better team – which the Knicks, even with their current ups and downs, are at this point in the season.

And please leave the Indiana underdog stories where they belong and where they are actually fun. Leave them to .

Who: New York Knicks (6-5) at Indiana Pacers (4-8)Date: Friday, November 13, 2026Place: Gainbridge Fieldhouse, Indianapolis, INFollow: @ptknicksblog and bsky
items.lbText:
Knicks will visit the Pacers during the group stage of the NBA Cup.

There are sports movies, there are even some good sports movies. And then there is Hoosiers .

As a basketball romantic you are definitely not flipping the channel when old ball coach Norman Dale a.k.a. Gene Hackman drives his 1951 Chevy Styleline Deluxe through the backwoods of Indiana all the way to the little town of Hickory, where he hopes to find a new life, new love and redemption. You let yourself be mesmerized by Angelo Pizzo’s and David Anspaugh’s timeless fairytale, by the very essence of “Hoosier Hysteria,” the beautiful yet tragic tribulations of high school sports, the rough, simple charm of small town America. And you enjoy every second of it, despite a rather predictable underdog story unfolding in front of your eyes that Hollywood has repeated many times over.

The current Indiana Pacers would kill for some of that predictability, the kind they expected going into this season. After a surprising Finals berth in 2025, their following year was doomed by Tyrese Haliburton’s ruptured Achilles. They punted on the next campaign and thought, with their point guard’s return, everything would return normal; that the half-court offense would run smooth as a “picket fence;” and that the jumpers would automatically fall like the ones by Jimmy Chitwood. But Haliburton (unfortunately) isn’t as quiet nor as down to earth as Mr. Chitwood, nor is an NBA season comparable to a Hollywood movie. It’s a lot more complicated than that.

The Pacers are finding that out the hard way. It only took testy Tyrese a handful of games until he got injured again (it’s a hamstring now) and his team sorely misses the All Star as their 4-8 record puts them in the lower region of the Eastern Conference. On Friday against the New York Knicks, Haliburton will also be reduced to trolling from the sidelines, and he won’t be able to right the wrongs that have plagued his squad so far this season. It’s a huge advantage for Mike Brown’s men as Haliburton is the straw that stirs the Apple Cider for Indiana. Most of their strategy revolves around his talent, his scoring and his distribution.

But it’s not like the Pacers are just struggling out of the gate because Hali has only played four games. Even with him they lost to Milwaukee, barely got by New Orleans and were annihilated by Dallas. Indiana can’t shoot threes (just over 33 percent), despite a traditionally fast pace their offense isn’t even close to functioning well (20th in offensive rating), and their D is nothing to write home about either (15th in the league). The Pacers are an atrocious rebounding team (29th in rebounding percentage) and they struggle mightily to hit their free throws.

Do they do anything well? They do, in fact, take good care of the ball and have a one of the best assist-to-turnover-ratios in the entire Association. Individually Pascal Siakam is enjoying a strong start to the season (22.7 points) and Andrew Nembhard has come firing out of the gates as well (17.1 points, 42.9 percent from downtown). A lot of guys are still left from that Finals team two years ago, so in theory they should know what it takes. And Rick Carlisle is still a tremendously respected coach, at least when he isn’t whining like a five year old who didn’t get his wish at Toys-R-Us.

The skipper really has his work cut out for him early in the year. New center Ivica Zubac, a classic, plodding back-to-basket big man with considerable post skills, hasn’t really found his place in an adjusted Pacers system that once was predicated on playing five-out at all costs. Continuity has also been a big issue as Carlisle has already started 11 different players, at times making it seem like the Pacers are still on their tanking ways from last year. They obviously aren’t and it should be noted that slow starts are nothing new for Indiana under Carlisle. Consider yourself warned.

With Friday’s game being another Cup contest you can bet that the Pacers will be highly motivated and our beloved Knicks better be ready for a hostile environment. Keep calm if Haliburton tries some stupid sideline voodoo as he certainly will when he senses a camera being on him. Feed Karl-Anthony Towns in a favorable matchup for him, let Brunson do his thing against Indiana’s supposed Brunson stoppers who always seem to just limit him to 35. Make use of your more talented depth, outshoot the struggling shooting team and control the tempo. Just show that you are the better team - which the Knicks, even with their current ups and downs, are at this point in the season.

And please leave the Indiana underdog stories where they belong and where they are actually fun. Leave them to Hoosiers .

items.title: Yankees’ Cam Schlittler, Ben Rice finish fourth, ninth in AL MVP voting
items.author: Matt Ferenchick
items.content:
By virtue of them not being announced as finalists, we knew that neither Cam Schlittler or Ben Rice were going to win the 2026 American League Most Valuable Player Award. However, we had a pretty good feeling that the Cy Young and the slugger were going to finish high in the voting. On Thursday night, the announcement came, and Schlittler and Rice finished in fourth and ninth place respectively.

The Astros’ Yordan Alvarez took home the award over fellow finalists Junior Caminero and Bobby Witt Jr. Alvarez ended up being the unanimous winner, receiving all 30 first place votes. Caminero was a clear second, receiving all but three second place votes.

One of the three second-place votes that didn’t go to Caminero did go to Schlittler — shout out to Dave Skretta of the Associated Press. The rest of his votes range somewhere between third and 10th. He only just narrowly missed being named a finalist, as he finished only seven points behind Witt for third. While a pitcher winning MVP has happened in recent memory, it can often be hard for them to get close considering that they have an award for themselves in the Cy Young. Finishing fourth matches Shane Bieber in 2020 — although there’s quite a big caveat on that one — for the best finish for a pure pitcher (sorry, Shohei) since Clayton Kershaw’s National League win in 2014.

As for Rice, he received two third-place votes himself, but all the rest of his ranged between fifth and 10th place. I think if I were voting, I would’ve had him higher up in ninth, but I am somewhat biased in the fact that I watch him every day.

Those were the only two Yankees to receive votes, which isn’t particularly shocking. You can view the full list here. For those curious, the Cubs’ Pete Crow-Armstrong was unsurprisingly named the unanimous winner in the NL.

There were certainly plenty of aspects to the Yankees’ 2026 season that were disappointing, but Schlittler and Rice certainly weren’t the reasons.
