items.title: You Don’t Have to Like 32s, But That Doesn’t Mean You’re Right
items.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
items.content: Forget the speculation and concepts; this is what it feels like to actually put a few hundred miles on a 32-inch gravel bike.
items.lbText:
I am going to lead with this at the top: this article is going to make a lot of people mad. I have seen the comments, the skepticism, the what-about-ery.

All of that is to say, forget your feelings . Thirty-two-inch gravel bikes make riding gravel so much more fun.

Up until this point, I have tried to remain neutral and objective. I have reported on 32-inch gravel tech since Sea Otter, and throughout that coverage I have couched my position in caveats, qualifiers, and fence-sitting.

I am not doing that anymore. After riding the Mosaic GT i55 32 gravel bike, I can say with clear eyes and a good conscience that all you haters are plain wrong. The bike is not perfect, but it is a phenomenal representation that the vast majority of 32-inch criticism is just not valid.

After hundreds of miles of riding across as many surfaces as I could find, the new wheels have clicked for me emphatically, and not for the way you might think. Speed, while top of mind in many of the 32-inch discussions, wasn’t the point that got me. It might have been faster, but ultimately that was less important than the other pull.

On gravel, the bike just cruises; that’s the only way I can distill it. It’s a dreamboat, holding traction well beyond smaller tires of similar tread and width, and carries so much speed every time it goes downhill. While I wasn’t at the front of the Big Sugar peloton, there were only one or two instances out of the 50 miles of racing where anyone could match the speed on downhills.

From a mix of a stable platform for pedaling through chunky terrain and preserving inertia through loose turns, I was constantly catching and passing people every time the road would tilt down, or the track got rough.

It was emphatically good at doing the things that smart people in the industry have been saying it would be well suited for.

Yeah, what about that handling! The 32-inch bike handled better than the vast majority of gravel bikes I have ridden, across the board. Sweeping bends? Yup. Chunky two-track? Absolutely. Twisty single track? Yes, with a bullet.

What the Mosaic 32 proved to me was how many people’s consideration of what makes good gravel bike handling is based around a deeply flawed premise. Largely, many bike riders think bikes with shorter wheelbases and steep angles have better handling, and long-wheelbase bikes are sluggish and cumbersome. In some circumstances, this might be true, but for any stretch of the definition of gravel racing, this paradigm is almost completely backwards.

Shorter geometry on gravel bikes does not make them turn better, accelerate faster, or handle more reliably. As long as the bike has balance, it can be long as hell and feel much, much more nimble.

There is a path for gravel bike design to have its cake and eat it, too. Current options with big tires and short chainstays, however, are like eating a bowl of frosting. Some might like it, but most would actually prefer the cake.

Ultimately, the myth about shorter chainstays helping handling runs so deep it is hard to push back on. It is a crowded hill that some of the biggest bike brands in the world seem set to die on. Yet, in short, shorter chainstays are susceptible to understeer. Understeer is what happens when a bike’s rear wheel tracks tighter around a corner than the front.

It is also the cause of most crashes that involve the front wheel slipping out or a rider blasting through the exit of a turn.

Another way of putting it is that understeer makes the rear wheel go straight when the front wheel is turning.

On mountain bikes, when the speeds are low and the turns are super tight, the longer wheelbase can backfire. But on gravel at speed, the longer wheelbase and chainstay will result in a much more rounded rear wheel trajectory and, ultimately, the ability to take more aggressive lines and speeds through cornering.

Thirty-two-inch wheels force bikes to have much longer chainstays. That is the underlying variable that immediately jumped out as I rode the bike. Even with the bigger wheels, it handled terrain better, even tight, twisty terrain the critics think would be the death of it.

Add in the better traction, increased stability, and quick front-end handling of a relatively steeper head tube angle, and the Mosaic 32 didn’t feel much different from some of my favorite 29-inch gravel bikes that pushed their rear ends to the appropriate length—it just held traction for a bit longer and rolled down hills just a bit faster.

As I mentioned, the Mosaic is not perfect. Thirty-two-inch wheels as a whole are not perfect. On road, the system is unequivocally slower. The weight, aero losses, and added height of the system are all things that outpace the rolling benefit on tarmac.

The weight is also unavoidable. Thirty-two-inch bikes are just bigger. There is just more material, and stiffness is harder to engineer around. It will always be a weight penalty, and that will make a difference on many routes. For Big Sugar, the rolling nature of the course made the 32 easily the better option for most riders. But for gravel rides with more sustained climbing and less gravel, the 21-pound build of the titanium 32-inch bike might be a slower overall option compared to a 17-pound 29-inch gravel bike.

I think because of these two aspects that won’t necessarily change in the big wheels’ favor, 29-inch will stick around, as there could easily be demand for both depending on what the consumer is looking for.

Speaking of consumers, the other fundamental criticism of 32-inch gravel bikes is how the bikes will scale down to smaller riders. While some of this concern is justified, I do think the prospect of 32-inch gravel for short riders is much better than for mountain biking.…

items.title: Sturdy Cycles Ditches 3D Printing for the New Fosse and Drove Titanium Bikes
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: The Somerset-based manufacturer is rolling out new road and gravel bikes at Rouleur Live along with a pivot to CNC-machined components and simplified sizing.
items.lbText:
Today at Rouleur Live, boutique UK builder Sturdy Cycles launched the Fosse and Drove titanium frame kits. Alongside the two new models, the brand is also announcing the reversal of a trend that many small builders have embraced in recent years.

The Somerset-based manufacturer is moving away from the 3D-printed junctions that characterized its earlier frames, replacing them with new titanium components that are CNC machined in-house. The machined pieces are then joined to drawn titanium tubes, with all welding and Cerakote finishing handled under the same roof. This change is significant because it reverses a trend in the bespoke titanium market.

For the past several years, additive manufacturing—specifically 3D printing titanium lugs—has been a favorite of small-batch frame builders. The process allows designers to create highly complex internal lattice structures to tune stiffness while keeping overall weight low. It also effectively eliminates the need for expensive dedicated tooling, making custom geometry significantly easier to scale.

Sturdy itself was a pioneer of this approach, heavily relying on printed junctions to deliver its bespoke frames. However, while additive manufacturing remains the go-to method for scaling production across the boutique market, Sturdy has found a different solution.

According to founder Tom Sturdy, moving the junction production to in-house CNC machining provides complete oversight of the build process. Specifically, milling from solid titanium allowed the brand to achieve tighter tolerances for bearing alignments, improve drivetrain efficiency, and produce a significantly smoother surface finish compared to raw 3D-printed parts.

This streamlined approach to manufacturing also extends to how the bikes are sized. Rather than drafting pure custom geometry for every order, Sturdy analyzed historical fit data from past made-to-measure builds to create a comprehensive sizing matrix. The brand categorized the sizes using baseline top tube measurements, then provided three distinct stack height options for each. When paired with the various stem and seatpost lengths included in the frame kit, the system is designed to provide the exact fit adjustability of a full custom frame, but with the straightforward purchasing experience of a standard retail bike.

Sturdy also noted a few other smart details aimed at solving the traditional annoyances of living with a titanium frame. Both bikes utilize phosphor-bronze inserts and threading at the seatpost clamp and thru-axles—areas where bare titanium components notoriously fuse together over time.

The Fosse is positioned as an endurance-friendly road machine. It features a relatively low bottom bracket to maintain stability when paired with modern, high-volume road tires. Utilizing an ENVE IN-Route Road carbon fork, the Fosse clears up to 35mm tires and is restricted to electronic groupsets.

For the dirt, the Drove features longer chainstays for climbing traction and stability at speed, paired with a front end designed to track straight over rough terrain. It utilizes an ENVE IN-Route Gravel carbon fork to clear 50mm tires and includes additional mounting points for a third bottle and a top tube bag.

To help riders navigate the 18 different sizing permutations, Sturdy introduced a suite of digital fitting tools. Prospective buyers can input their current bike’s coordinates to find the correct size , use a bar position calculator to map out their cockpit, and visually overlay the Fosse or Drove geometry directly over their existing frame.

Once the fit is nailed down, buyers can use an online selector to customize the aesthetics. The standard finish, which is included in the base price, features shot-peened raw titanium across the frame, stem, and seatpost, accented by a brushed or Cerakote downtube logo. For riders who want a more individualized look, Sturdy offers custom one- and two-color Cerakote themes for an additional £720, while fully bespoke finishes start at £2,400.

Both frames are available to order now. Because each frame kit is made to order, Sturdy notes a lead time of roughly six weeks, with the first deliveries expected in late 2026. Frame kits for both models are priced at £6,000 (including UK VAT), while complete SRAM Force builds push past the £10,000 mark. Visit the Sturdy website for more info.

items.title: Former US champion Stephen Bassett 'knows what it takes to win' and leads group of seven new riders at growing domestic squad with criterium focus
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
US road veterans Stephen Bassett and Caleb Classen headline seven new signings in 2027 for Chaney Windows and Doors as the domestic elite team postures for a more versatile roster on a "crit-heavy race schedule".

The duo competed the last three seasons for Project Echelon Racing and will anchor an 11-rider roster. Former rider Owen Gillott, who won the American Criterium Cup sprint classification title the last two years, will move into the role of director sportif.

"Stephen and Caleb bring the experience and race sense to lead us in the criteriums that define our 2027 calendar," said Nick Hand, general manager of Chaney Windows and Doors.

"Stephen knows what it takes to win, and we’re excited to bring that championship experience into our 2027 campaign. With experience competing against some of the strongest fields in North America and Europe, Caleb brings another level of depth and versatility to our squad."

Bassett joins the team with 14 years of racing experience, including a signature title in 2024 as the USPro Criterium National Champion. Last year he had two stage podiums at the Tour de Bloom, GC second place at the Tucson Bicycle Classic and won the one-day Café Hollander Tosa Village Classic.

Classen built his 10-year career in stage racing, where he finished fifth on GC at both Joe Martin Stage Race and Tour of the Gila. In 2025, he placed second on a stage at Volta a Portugal. He brings power to one-day races, showcasing his talent with a win at Colorado's iconic Iron Horse Bicycle Classic.

Cameron Adams, 24, was a guest rider last year who scored top-10s at both pro races at the Salt Lake Criterium. Originally from Guatemala, Demsy Cifuentes, 23, joins from Parks Law Firm, where he won Hotter 'n Hell last year.

Under-23 riders include Carlos Perez Calzada of Spain and US duo Jake Zyromski (19) and Tyler Mlujeak (22). Perez, 21, moves from Savannah College of Art and Design where he a trio of collegiate podiums in 2026, including Sunny King Criterium.

Riders returning to the squad include US Masters criterium champion Tim Smith, former track rider Lance Abshire, crit specialist Gabe Porterfield, and 22-year-old Jura Gerlach, who was fourth for Milligan University at the USA Cycling Gravel National Championships in the men's open category.

Based out of St. Louis, Missouri, the team begins a third season with a focus on domestic road and track racing with plans to add a gravel programme. Equipment partner State Bicycle Company will provide new aero gravel frames for the new calendar of off-road.

"Our goal has always been to be a multi-disciplined team," said Scott Chaney, team owner. "We began as an international track squad before branching off into racing crits. State is very invested in the gravel world, and we wanted to have riders who could showcase their amazing products."

Hand told that Classen and Bassett will be supplied State gravel bikes and take part in a few events, but Gerlach will be the "official" gravel rider next year. Gerlach has competed three times at Unbound Gravel 200, his best finish fourth in 2025 in the open category.

The squad will have a small camp in Phoenix, Arizona in the winter, then focus on a full training camp in Austin, Texas to coincide with Pace Bend weekend, March 13-14, and then launch the season officially in April at Sunny King Criterium in Alabama.

"We are focused on getting everyone vibing together and making sure management is getting all the kinks out, whether that's equipment, support, or whatever. We just want to ensure these guys have everything they need to be as successful as possible," Hand said.

items.title: Video: Watch a Day in the Life of Sepp Kuss
items.author: ahood
items.content: Off-season doc featuring American star Sepp Kuss just cracked Visma’s 20 most-watched YouTube videos. Have you watched it?
items.lbText:
A new video featuring Kuss is taking off on YouTube. (Photo: Visma-Lease a Bike)

Visma-Lease a Bike’s new “Day in the Life” documentary has passed 210,000 views by Thursday, giving fans a look at the American’s off-season lifestyle at home in Andorra with his wife, Noemi, and daughter, Martina.

Think quiet family time, home-cooked meals, and grand tour trophies tucked into corners. And, oh yeah, lots of bikes.

The video is taking off. Visma officials said it cracked the team’s 20 most-watched YouTube videos within 24 hours.

Kuss — the last American to win a grand tour after his 2023 Vuelta a España victory — also looks back on the 2026 season when he rode the Giro, Tour, and Vuelta, and won a stage at the Giro to complete the grand tour stage win sweep.

“Mentally it was easier than a normal season, because you have really concrete blocks and concrete goals,” he said. “Between that, it’s a pretty simple routine and easy living.”

Watch the full documentary on Visma’s YouTube channel .

items.title: Winspace Flips the Script With a Pure Hype Tease for the C6 Endurance Bike
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: The Chinese manufacturer stepped into Rouleur Live to show off its new 40mm-clearance road machine, taking a page straight out of the Western marketing playbook.
items.lbText:
Today, Winspace is teasing the C6 endurance bike. To be clear, the brand isn’t actually launching the bike or even announcing a release date—just teasing that it exists and will come soon. In this case, that tactic is as much the news as the actual bike.

Winspace is part of the new wave of Chinese manufacturers that have come to Western markets with impressive specs for the price and built real brand recognition. Now, the brand is taking a page straight out of the Western marketing handbook. At this week’s Rouleur Live in London—an event that traditionally serves as a boutique, high-end showcase for premium cycling culture and bespoke craftsmanship—Winspace is showing off the C6, but doing so without actually releasing any concrete data.

What little information the brand did provide positions the C6 as something along the lines of the Enve Fray or Cannondale Synapse. Billed as a performance endurance bike, the C6 frame aims to bridge the gap between race-day efficiency and all-day comfort. To accomplish this, Winspace claims the bike pairs a rigid lower frame designed for efficient power transfer with a vertically compliant rear end that utilizes dropped seatstays, a bowed seat tube, and a D-shaped seatpost to absorb road vibration. The geometry takes a similar dual-purpose approach, combining a slightly upright riding position to reduce hand pressure with steering geometry tuned for quick, precise handling. Most notably, the bike features clearance for up to 40 mm tires, positioning it not as a gravel bike of old, but as a road bike at the forefront of big tires for fast rides.

“We designed the C6 around how riders use their bikes today,” Head of Design Mike Pryde stated. “The geometry, frame compliance, and tire clearance were developed together to deliver responsive handling, predictable control, and the ride quality needed for sustained performance over longer distances.”

The non-launch shows a level of marketing sophistication not always seen from Chinese manufacturers, who tend to prefer moving quickly, releasing new bikes regularly, and letting the market see what works. Western brands have traditionally moved much slower and leaned heavily on pre-release hype. Even relatively fast-moving Van Rysel soft-launched a bike at the show representing over two years in development. But while Van Rysel shared essentially all the details—despite the bike not being available until 2027—Winspace is taking the opposite approach. The brand is almost completely teasing the C6, holding back its full specifications, build options, and pricing until Nov. 18.

For now, you can visit the Winspace website for more information about the brand, but that’s all we currently know about the C6.

items.title: I was wrong about Cam Schlittler
items.author: Peter Brody
items.content:
The Yankees officially have their seventh AL Cy Young Award winner in franchise history! Cam Schlittler rightly claimed a clean sweep of the highest pitching award in the land, becoming the third Yankee after Ron Guidry in 1978 and Gerrit Cole in 2023 to win the award in unanimous fashion. He fended off fellow frontrunner Dylan Cease with a stretch of late season excellence to author the best pitching season in franchise history since Guidry’s extraterrestrial award-winning campaign, finishing the year 14-6 in 33 starts, with a 1.95 ERA (215 ERA+), 2.56 FIP, 0.92 WHIP, and 239 strikeouts in 193.2 innings, leading all AL starters with 6.2 fWAR and setting a single-season franchise record with 21 starts allowing one or fewer runs. After enduring a 22 year drought since Roger Clemens took home the prize in 2001, the Yankees have now claimed two of the last four AL Cy Young’s between Cole and now Schlittler.

With Schlittler’s meteoric rise from an obscure draft pick to unheralded prospect to playoff hero to now the best pitcher in the AL, I would like to offer a of sorts. I am not ashamed to admit that I was wrong about the Yankees’ now-undisputed ace.

First, I’ll give myself a small bit of credit for identifying Schlittler as the team’s breakout pitcher during 2025 spring training. While certainly impressed by his high octane velocity that seemingly came out of nowhere, I had my reservations about the repeatability of his mechanics and the resulting lack of command I believed that conferred. I was sharply critical during his first six or so starts during the regular season in 2025 about what I perceived as him being a thrower rather than a pitcher, his imprecise command, and the erratic nature of his slider. I went back to the time period surrounding those half-dozen starts to pull a few of my own quotes evaluating his up-and-down performances that yielded a 3.94 ERA, 5.26 FIP, and 10.8-percent walk rate at the time:

“Cam Schlittler’s principal issue since being promoted to the big league rotation has been a complete lack of command over his secondary pitches.”

“For all the velocity he possesses, far too often Schlittler seemingly has no idea where the slider is going which effectively removes the pitch as a reasonable selection. No amount of velocity in the world will then save you once you become a fastball-only pitcher.”

“The command of the slider was an issue with too many staying elevated or in the heart of the zone. He actually reworked the pitch in the offseason, adding velocity at the expense of movement — he even said during the postgame that he now considers the pitch to be a cutter rather than a gyro slider as Statcast currently has it categorized. I’m not convinced the current version of the pitch can be a reliable swing-and-miss option and I’d like to see him expand the use of the sweeper in advantageous counts.”

“His cutter was a home run machine when he first came up owing to a propensity to miss middle-middle.”

Suffice to say I did not envision at that point that roughly 15 months later, Schlittler would be unanimously selected as the 2026 Cy Young winner. And all the credit goes to him for not only identifying the areas of his game that needed improvement, but actively seeking help from the Yankees pitching coaches and his veteran teammates in the rotation. It is said that Schlittler is among the most eager and proactive pitchers in the organization at pouring over the pitch metric data and high-speed video to find the subtle adjustments for fine-tuning grip, finger positioning, release, and arm path mechanics, squeezing every drop out of his physical gifts.

One of the first things I noticed this year was a simplifying of his delivery. In 2025, it seemed he relied too much on brute arm speed to supply velocity, the longer arm path and more maximum effort delivery robbing him of precise fastball command. In 2026, he learned to engage his lower half more, sinking his hips to draw more power from his leg drive. This allowed him to shorten his takeaway and turned his somewhat loopy arm path into a more compact stroke, which not only sharpened his command but gave him access to a few more ticks on the heater, allowing him to touch 101 mph. With a more repeatable delivery, Schlittler found he could live on the top shelf of the strike zone with relative ease.

Schlittler’s receptiveness to feedback is super impressive, especially for a young player with rapidly growing hype surrounding him. He sought out Cole before the season, and a conversation they had about reshaping his slider into a cutter and throwing it as hard as he could unlocked a new level for Schlittler. Thus, he was able to transform probably the weakest facet of his game — a slider with unpredictable command — into one of the best cutters in the game, which also boosted the effectiveness of his four-seamer and sinker given the way its movement diverged from that latter pair of pitches. Adding the cutter is what allowed him to excel while throwing a fastball variant 89.3-percent of the time.

What impressed me most — and another piece of overwhelming evidence that Schlittler is indeed a pitcher and not just a thrower — is his constant quest to find that next level. Not content to simply rest on the laurels of his three overpowering fastballs, Schlittler evolved his game in the second half of the season by developing a unicorn curveball that could play off his new-found mastery of the top of the zone. Facing a Red Sox team fully expecting him to go heavy fastball when they met in the AL Wild Card Series, Schlittler threw a career-high 32 curveballs to completely confound their gameplan. This ability to be a step ahead of the opposition to me is evidence of Schlittler’s dedication to his craft.

It absolutely delights me to say how wrong I was about Schlittler in his first taste of the bigs. More and more pitchers these days can touch triple digits with their fastball. It is the rare player like Schlittler who is never satisfied with his physical gifts, and this insatiable push to keep becoming a better version of himself is why this unanimous AL Cy Young might not be the last of his career.

items.title: I Ditched Structured Training for a Year. Here’s Why I’m Going Back.
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: Skipping winter intervals sounded great until I saw the results on the road. Here is what I learned, and a better way to build your off-season fitness.
items.lbText:
Welcome to Dropped , a new weekly road and gravel cycling newsletter from Velo that brings you the latest ideas we’re debating endlessly on group rides, and a look behind the scenes of our coverage.

I ride a lot, but I‘m not a WorldTour racer. Like most of the people reading this, I have a family and other obligations besides the bike. I also love to ride, and personally, I like to go as fast as possible for as long as possible. You may or may not share that exact goal, but I bet we can all agree on one thing: intervals are not fun. I have a VO2 max workout on the calendar today, and it fills me with dread, not excitement.

Given my preference for actually enjoying my bike, I looked back at my ride history near the tail end of 2025 and took stock. I’ve been tracking my power for about six years, and every single season I hit an FTP around 250-260 in the late summer. I also rarely stick to a strict, structured training plan to get there; I generally just ride a lot and do intervals that I think make sense.

That set of facts filled me with a special kind of hubris and hope. My job, in some ways, is to test things that people hold to be true without thought. I don’t like blindly trusting general knowledge. Plus, again, intervals are miserable. So, I decided to run an experiment: for the last year, I didn’t do intervals.

It’s not that I did nothing hard; I just shifted from structured intervals to steady-state riding. Over the winter, my “intensity” was a hard 100k Zwift group ride on Sundays, plus the occasional 1-hour Zwift race. When summer arrived, my hard workout became a 40-minute block at about 200 watts. I always kept a long 6-hour-plus ride on the weekend, and the rest of the week was whatever I felt like doing.

The result of this experiment was a 30-watt FTP loss and shaving about 300 watts off my sprint. It’s common knowledge that you lose top-end punch without intervals, but those are the actual numbers. And that happened without a drop in volume as my year-to-date totals across 2025 and 2026 are virtually identical as of Nov 4th (around 7,300 miles and 440 hours). Same volume, different training, massive losses.

Or is it a massive loss? Remember that my goal is ultra-endurance distances. When I isolate my outdoor rides over 80 miles and adjust for elevation, my average speed is the exact same 16.3 mph. Maybe it doesn’t matter?

There are problems with that, though. I don’t only ride alone, and my high-end power is gone. I now get dropped at the mere hint of a climb and have zero chance in a town-line sprint. I’m your guy for the back half of a double century, but if you were ever curious about what actually happens when you ditch structured training, I did the experiment for you.

There’s no getting around those results. Structured training is a must and, like I said, I have a VO2 max session tonight.

I have a suggestion, though. I’m not a coach, and this is not for anyone who is focused on racing, but if your goal is to be generally fast and ride long distances, winter base miles may not be the best approach. For the last 15-ish years—this recent experiment aside—I’ve followed an approach called reverse periodization and it’s worked for me. It’s hardly groundbreaking, but it’s all about enjoying yourself when it makes sense and getting faster when that actually helps motivation.

At its core, this simply flips the traditional training calendar. Historically, cyclists spent the winter grinding out long, slow base miles and saved high-intensity intervals for the spring and summer. Reversing the order of operations takes advantage of the desire for short intensity in the winter (it’s far easier to make yourself complete a workout than it is to just enjoy a ride when you aren’t going anywhere) before training seamlessly shifts to the long outdoor endurance rides you actually want to be doing anyway.

Doing it this way also aligns perfectly with biology. Your body can’t be at peak fitness all year. Given that summer is when there are cycling events, winter is when you naturally need to detrain a bit. What that actually looks like used to mean one of two things: either do something else like cross-country skiing, or riding in the cold.

In 2026, changing sports is obviously still an option, but far more people ride indoors. The catch is that indoor riding is still best taken in smaller chunks. That creates an opportunity. Instead of forcing miserable, long, slow rides while staring at a screen, you take on smaller, more intense rides.

And executing that is easier now than it ever was in the past. The reason this approach works so well today is the significant upheaval in the technology of indoor riding. In the past, indoor intervals meant staring at a clock on rollers or a basic cycling computer. There simply weren’t high-quality virtual ride systems like TrainerRoad, Zwift, Rouvy, or TrainingPeaks Virtual. There also weren’t high-tech trainers and indoor bikes that made it easy to ride inside and follow a specific plan.

It all adds up to a system that just makes sense. As endurance coach Andrew Simmons points out over on TrainingPeaks , the traditional model was built for racers who need sharp, punchy power in July at a time when smart trainers and virtual worlds didn’t exist. For endurance riders, it’s backward. The golden rule of training is specificity: the closer you get to your target season, the more your riding should look like what you actually want to do. That means if you aren’t a racer, it makes sense to swap the order and you stand to lose nothing doing it this way.…

items.title: Record $800,000 prize purse in 2027 'continues to elevate the standard' for Life Time Grand Prix series and events with Unbound, Leadville and Big Sugar each boosting payouts
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
A record $800,000 will be offered across seven individual races and the overall prize payout for the Life Time Grand Prix in 2027, organisers of the off-road series confirmed Thursday. This reflects a 36% increase from this past season, and is more than triple the original prize purse from the inaugural 2022 season.

The overall series purse jumps from $350,000 in 2026 to $400,000, while the other $400,000 will be spread across each stop on the calendar, spread across April to October, an increase from $240,000 last season. All prizes are paid for the top 10 in races and the series, split eventually between the men's and women's pro fields.

"It just continues to elevate the standard. And we think we've seen great success. We want to elevate the stature and the attraction to the Life Time Grand Prix and the individual events. We've been able to do that with continuing to increase the prize purse for both the individual events and the Grand Prix as a whole," Kimo Seymour, president of Events and Media at Life Time, told .

Life Time launched the invitation-only series in 2022 as the popularity of gravel and endurance mountain bike races surged. Specialized Off-road duo Keegan Swenson and Sofia Gomez Villafañe have won the overall pro titles four times each across the first five years. Swenson won $25,000 for first place in the inaugural year, while Villafañe earned the same amount with her first title in 2023.

In October, they earned $50,000 each for first place. However, next year whoever lands on the top steps will earn $40,000 each. The pool of money now distributes payouts more evenly across the rest of the top 10, with riders going seventh through 10th now receiving $10,000 or more each. Life Time says restructuring the purse was about "incentivizing season-long competition".

"If we want professional off-road cycling to grow, we have to get serious about how athletes make a living. As the Series becomes more successful, the athletes should share in that success. By putting more money into every race and spreading those dollars deeper into the field, we're creating more opportunities for more riders, not just the handful at the very top," Michelle Duff, co-director of the Life Time Grand Prix, stated in a press release.

Maybe more significant are the individual race payouts, now equal to the series itself in total money and moving from just the top five to the top 10. A total of $80,000 will be on offer at Unbound Gravel 200, Leadville Trail 100 MTB and Life Time Big Sugar Classic.

Last year, the purses at Unbound Gravel and Leadville Trail 100 MTB were $60,000 each, and Big Sugar was $30,000. In fact, Unbound and Leadville did not offer prize money for pro fields until two years ago.

The other four events - Sea Otter Classic, Chequamegon MTB Festival, The Rad Dirt Fest and Little Sugar MTB - will pay out $40,000 each. That is a 33% increase for three of the races, while The Rad Dirt Fest has an enormous boost from a previous payout of $2,5000, since it was last part of the series in 2024. And, those US dollars are for any athlete who finishes in the top 10, not just the Grand Prix riders.

"I have to give a lot of the credit to the athletes. You know, we spend so much time with athletes, hearing feedback and getting advice and guidance and suggestions. One of the suggestions was about offerings at individual events, not so much on the Grand Prix. So that's why we've chosen to split it equitably between the Grand Prix and the individual events. It's significant enough that big-name athletes are starting to show up," Seymour explained to

"There needs to be better opportunities for the athletes to make money. I think with the new distribution this year will continue to draw some of those big international names as well, which only brings more eyeballs, more viewership, more fan engagement, and hopefully more, you know, more sponsor investment."

Where does the money come from for the $800,000? Life Time owns all the races in the series, so has complete control of not just logistics but broadcast rights and sponsorships. Seymour said that an emphasis on social media engagement was the biggest component of their portfolio, which includes the robust live stream shown on the YouTube channel.

"It's not a sponsor-specific prize purse. It just comes out of our overall budget for the Grand Prix. We're able to monetize the series more and more each year, as it's grown overall. So, primarily YouTube engagement, we're able to drive more sponsorship or advertising dollars against the series," Seymour said.

"Probably more than anything, it's been our YouTube views. I think we're over five million views this year on Life Time specific [channel] and Grand Prix content that we've put out."

Seymour confirmed to that they planned to offer live broadcasts for five of the seven events in 2027, the elements to bring video from mountain bike events at Chequamegon and Little Sugar still being worked out.

The Life Time Grand Prix will continue as an invitation-only field of 50 riders, the rules for participation also evolving to a more performance-driven pathway. The compensation portion of the series extends beyond the podium, and for a second year, athletes who complete the series and finish 11th through 25th will receive a $2,500 finisher bonus, which is outside the primary prize purse. Introduced in 2026, this structure rewards the riders who race all season.

The opening round of the 2027 Life Time Grand Prix will be Thursday, April 15 in Monterey, California, for Life Time Sea Otter Classic Gravel.

items.title: Life Time Grand Prix Increases Prize Purse by Over $200K
items.author: Will Tracy
items.content: The premier off-road race series in North America is investing in its athletes as it heads into its sixth season, increasing payouts by 36% and distributing them across more racers.
items.lbText:
The Life Time Grand Prix prize purse is increasing significantly in 2027. (Photo: Life Time)

Racers in the Life Time Grand Prix can look forward to bigger pay days in 2027.

Life Time announced Thursday that the premier off-road race series in North America will have an $800,000 USD prize purse in 2027, a 36 percent increase over 2026’s $590,000 purse. The move signals continued growth for the series and an investment in its athletes as it heads into its sixth season.

“One of the things we’re trying to do is kind of fundamentally change the business model of professional cycling,” Kimo Seymour, president, events and media at Life Time, told Velo .

“Athletes don’t get an opportunity to participate in the success of the events. And it’s no secret how broken the whole pure sponsorship model of professional cycling is.

“I’m like, well, why can’t we change it a little bit? If we can generate more revenue, we ought to be able to figure out a way to share more of that revenue with the athletes. I think it is a way for us to give back some of the success we’re seeing with the series.”

Payouts have increased for each of the seven individual races in the series, which runs from April to October, as well as for most of the top finishers overall in the series. Of the $800,000 purse, half is dedicated to payouts for the individual races, and the other half to the top overall finishers in the series.

As has been the case since the series’ first year in 2022, the money will be split equally between the men’s and women’s fields, totaling $400,000 to each.

Unbound Gravel and Leadville continue to have the largest prize purses in the series, growing from $60,000 per race to $80,000. Life Time is substantially increasing the prize money for Big Sugar, the final race of the series, raising it from $30,000 to $80,000. It signals the race’s growth and increased importance.

“Our feeling was that Big Sugar is, for lack of a better term, it’s just getting bigger and bigger each year,” Seymour said. “It’s an important one on the calendar for the Grand Prix. We’re getting more and more non-Grand Prix pro athletes showing up at that event as well.”

The remaining races in the series—Sea Otter Classic, Chequamegon MTB Festival, The Rad Dirt Fest and Little Sugar MTB—will pay $40,000 per race. That’s up from $30,000 for all those events excluding The Rad, which sees its payout increase significantly from $5,000 as it returns to the Life Time Grand Prix in 2027.

The payouts at individual races now run deeper into the results sheet, to 10th place overall, up from the top five spots in 2026. Depending on the race, individual race winners will earn the same $10,000 or $5,000 prizes as in 2026, with bigger paydays spread across the remaining top 10 athletes.

The top-two overall finishers in the series will see their winnings reduced from $50,000 to $40,000 and $33,000 to $30,000, while spots 3-10 will see their winnings increase by at least a few thousands dollars per position.

Many of these decisions on how to distribute the prize purse have come from the athletes themselves, Seymour said.

“We got a lot of great feedback from the athletes and spreading the prize purse at the individual events down 10 deep was one of their suggestions,” he said. “And then also spreading it a little more equitably in the top 10 overall in the Grand Prix was another suggestion that came from the athletes.”

Life Time’s expenses for the series are about an even split between prize money and the costs of producing and promoting the events, said Seymour. Life Time has opted to continue to keep that investment equal as the series grows, seeing value in investing in the athletes who also help drive the media impressions that grow the series.

Seymour envisions the Life Time Grand Prix possibly reaching a point where it can create a revenue sharing model of sorts, more akin to one of the major North American sports leagues than traditional cycling models as we currently know them.

“At some point, that’s my dream, is that we would get [to revenue sharing],” he said. “We do that to some extent where now we’re paying all athletes that finish the series.”

Racers outside the top-10 overall but who finish the series in 2027 will get $2,500, continuing the finisher bonus that the series introduced in 2026.

items.title: MotoGP makes major US TV step with ESPN deal
items.author: Simon Patterson
items.content:
MotoGP has penned a new two-year deal for 2027 with broadcaster ESPN that will finally give the series a more permanent United States TV home, after a series of somewhat confusing contracts in recent seasons jumping around between different channels, platforms, and broadcasters.

The new deal, which will cover coverage not just in the US but also across Latin America, means ESPN becomes the exclusive rights holder for MotoGP, with a commitment to providing live or same-day coverage of every round.

Perhaps most importantly given the changing media landscape of recent years, it will also bring MotoGP onto one of the market’s major streaming platforms as it will appear on Disney+.

The news should come as welcome relief to US fans after quite a bit of uncertainty in recent years over where exactly to watch MotoGP.

Prior to 2020, the championship had a deal with BeIN Sports in which its team attended multiple races in person, before a move to NBC for four years.

But while that deal was notable for being with a major network, it meant MotoGP coverage jumping around between channels, with many races not airing live. A new deal for 2024 with TNT Sports (announced only hours before the start of the season) didn’t prove to be substantially different.

MotoGP moved to Fox in 2025, again announced only hours before the opening session of the first weekend, and again coverage moved around between channels, with this year’s American Grand Prix at Austin airing live on Fox Business.

With that in mind, the new ESPN deal should come as welcome news not just to MotoGP fans but to the series’ new Liberty Media owner, by providing a valuable growth platform as it attempts to replicate its success with Formula 1 in the US market.

"This agreement with ESPN marks an important milestone in MotoGP's growth strategy across the Americas,” said MotoGP’s deputy CEO Carlos Ezpleleta. 

“ESPN's position as one of the world's leading sports broadcasters, combined with its strong connection with audiences across the United States and Latin America, makes it the ideal platform for us to continue expanding MotoGP's reach and bring the sport closer to millions of people. 

“This is an exciting opportunity to introduce MotoGP to new audiences while continuing to serve our passionate existing fanbase through one of the most influential sports media brands in the world."

items.title: Pirelli Unveils New Colorways for Its High-Volume Road Tires
items.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
items.content: The new options will come in light tan and dark brown sidewalls.
items.lbText:
The tire that revolutionized the “thick-slick” movement is back with more color combinations, as Pirelli just released two new sidewall colors for its P-Zero Race TLR tire in 35 and 40mm widths.

The new Classic and Retro colorways add panache to the fast-rolling tire, giving road riders more options on gravel bikes and large-clearance all-road or endurance bikes.

Pirelli’s P Zero Race TLR is made in Italy and pairs its Speedcore technology with a fast and supple 120 TPI casing to boost rolling efficiency, flexibility, and durability. That creates the ingredients for Pirelli to produce speed at tire widths that previously were reserved for heavy, slow, or treaded tires.

The new sidewall options are available now. For more information, check out Pirelli’s website .

items.title: Carrick sacked by Manchester United with team in Premier League relegation zone – as it happened
items.author: John Brewin; Luke McLaughlin and John Ashdown
items.content:
The latest news and reaction as Manchester United look for a new head coach after only only three victories so far this season

“After going through the Moyes season,” writes Hugh, “the dross football of Mourinho and Van Gaal, the moments-years of Solskjaer, the Rangnick surgery that never was, the middling Ten Hag, the baffling Amorim, and now a decent man thrust into the meat grinder, this is the first year it’s been genuinely hard to watch Man Utd with any emotion.

“And it’s not because of the football. It’s that the Glazer ownership and Ratcliffe mismanagement has met the Man City revelations, meaning it’s hard to see the point anymore. £1bn taken out of the club while others were illicitly pumping in roughly the same. A club drained of life, hollowed out … I can take crap football, but I can’t take this anymore.”

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
The Manchester United Supporters’ Trust (MUST) earlier issued a statement following Carrick’s dismissal pinning the blame for poor results firmly on the ownership. In full below:

Michael Carrick’s departure marks another depressing moment for Manchester United. We thank him for his service and for restoring hope during the second half of last season. His standing among supporters remains undiminished.

The reason Manchester United fans have continued to support Michael Carrick in recent weeks is that they know that responsibility for United’s problems do not primarily rest with him or indeed his predecessors as manager.

The Glazers’ debt-funded takeover continues to burden the club. When INEOS came in they promised sporting excellence, but yet with repeated changes in football leadership we have seen anything but.

It is time for the owners to explain themselves and show some accountability.

But the discontent at United is not just about matters on the pitch. Far from it.

Aggressive ticketing policies have further damaged relations with supporters. Treating loyal fans principally as a source of revenue undermines their identity and the bond with the team that sustains support through difficult times. Supporters are being asked to pay the price for the owners’ mismanagement as well as their stadium ambitions through higher charges and diminished rights.

The earlier Stretford End banner declaring “The way you treat us is a disgrace” was a warning. The unprecedented scale of the booing at Old Trafford, alongside public criticism from senior players in recent weeks, now points to a deeper deterioration. These are signs of a club becoming more divided, with the bond between supporters, players and those running Manchester United under increasing strain.

MUST warned publicly in January 2025 that alienating supporters risked a downward spiral of worsening atmosphere, performances and financial outcomes. Our subsequent Telegraph article urged Sir Jim Ratcliffe to break that “doom loop” by bringing supporters with him. Those warnings remain painfully relevant.

The owners must allow senior club management to change direction: show accountability, rebuild trust, listen to supporters and recognise that their loyalty is fundamental to football success. Another change of head coach cannot repair what the ownership continues to undermine.

items.title: Fitness, Fernandes and a back four: how next head coach can reignite Manchester United | Will Unwin
items.author: Will Unwin
items.content:
Michael Carrick’s replacement must find solutions on the pitch and pressure the hierarchy to accept a share of blame

One of the final images of Michael Carrick’s time in charge will be of him standing in the rain on the Old Trafford touchline watching his side succumb to Bournemouth, while his sullen captain sat unused on the bench. Bruno Fernandes was dropped after calling out his head coach’s tactics, although Carrick said it was for football reasons. It was the second combustible television interview in as many Champions League games after Lisandro Martínez pointed the finger at the director of football, Jason Wilcox, for failing to provide a squad suitable for fighting on all fronts.

items.lbText:
Michael Carrick’s replacement must find solutions on the pitch and pressure the hierarchy to accept a share of blame

One of the final images of Michael Carrick’s time in charge will be of him standing in the rain on the Old Trafford touchline watching his side succumb to Bournemouth , while his sullen captain sat unused on the bench. Bruno Fernandes was dropped after calling out his head coach’s tactics, although Carrick said it was for football reasons. It was the second combustible television interview in as many Champions League games after Lisandro Martínez pointed the finger at the director of football, Jason Wilcox, for failing to provide a squad suitable for fighting on all fronts.

Fernandes was soon back in the fold, and Martínez apologised for his outburst , but it is clear internal discipline is an issue and will be central to getting the team back on track. United will always draw more attention than almost any other club in the world and creating a circus around a failing team merely complicates matters when there are already enough problems to sort out on the pitch. The players need to harness their anger to ensure they create headlines for performances, not interviews.

One player Jason Wilcox could claim as a recruitment success was Senne Lammens but the goalkeeper’s form has joined that of his teammates in the gutter. The Belgian endured a horror show for Bournemouth’s third goal when he rushed out of his area, and he made two errors in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa . Leny Yoro was another to make a terrible mistake against Bournemouth, while Diogo Dalot’s efforts as a makeshift left-back can be categorised as somewhere between woeful and inept. No team in Europe’s top five leagues have conceded more than United’s 30 in all competitions, which is clearly a worry.

Morale is at rock bottom but the chopping and changing in defence is creating more uncertainty. The new head coach should pick a back four and stick with it where possible. If Harry Maguire’s experience is deemed mandatory, he needs pace around him to make up for what he lacks. Luke Shaw’s absence has created a left-back tombola as Dalot, Ayden Heaven and Noussair Mazraoui have been placed there.

Benjamin Sesko’s injury has cost United a No 9 for most of the season and Joshua Zirkzee has rarely been trusted in the role. Matheus Cunha gave it a go as a false 9 and Bryan Mbeumo was tried as a more traditional centre-forward but without much success either. Cunha has become more productive in a deeper role behind the striker, cutting in from the left as he did at Wolves, but United require someone to be a classic No 9, someone who can occupy defenders and be serviced by deliveries from wide. Zirkzee, for his faults, has been a presence when used in recent weeks and scored against Aston Villa. If a new coach can rebuild his confidence, the Dutchman could provide a short-term solution. Alternatively, greater demands should be made of Marcus Rashford to play through the middle.

A mix-and-match of expletives were aimed at those above Carrick at recent home games. Wilcox has taken most of the individual criticism, but the ownership were told in no uncertain terms to sell up. The Glazers have been instrumental in driving the club downwards in recent years and Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s investment and involvement in football operations have yielded little success.

Carrick was the face of the operation, as the new head coach will be, and he needs to put pressure on someone at the top to speak to the media to explain why the club is in such a mess because it is unfair to expect the coach to do so. United fans know the person in the dugout cannot take all the blame and someone else has to be publicly accountable.

Three central midfielders and a backup goalkeeper did not make for an inspiring summer when everyone knew United’s squad required improvement in numerous positions. Andrey Santos, Carlos Baleba and Youri Tielemans started together against Bournemouth and offered no evidence for why so much was spent on them.

Whoever comes in needs to be clear about what is required, whether in the winter or summer windows, because the deficiencies in the squad mean United cannot compete on all fronts and are struggling to cope with the rigours of the Premier League. A new left-back and striker are a given, but there is plenty more work to be done.

Outrunning the opposition does not guarantee success but United have looked pedestrian on far too many occasions this season. This could explain the number of slow starts to games in recent times: in the Champions League against Atlético Madrid and Como they conceded in the first and second minute respectively, and were two down at home to Roma after 17 minutes last week. Worse still, Aston Villa, aided by errors, were two goals ahead within four minutes at Old Trafford, giving United a monumental task to turn things around. The players deserve credit for finding some fight to do so but need to make life easier for themselves because it does not take a genius to work out starting with a deficit is ill-advised. They will face a fiery atmosphere at Anfield, and that will be a fine place to show a shift in dynamic.

items.title: Van Rysel Drops Weight and Adds Aero to the New RCR-R Lineup
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: Developed directly with the Decathlon CMA CGM WorldTour team, the second-generation RCR-R platform drops weight and blends lessons from the dedicated aero bike.
items.lbText:
Today Van Rysel is launching a new version of the RCR-R and RCR-R PRO all-around race bikes. This is a continuation of the work that started when Van Rysel, Decathlon’s in-house performance cycling brand, sprang to life in Lille, France, in 2019. The brand then really catapulted into the global spotlight when it took over as the bike sponsor for the Decathlon CMA CGM WorldTour team in 2024.

As part of that sponsorship, Van Rysel splits its lineup between the RCR-F dedicated aero platform and the RCR as a lightweight generalist. Today’s launch is an attempt to bring what Van Rysel learned from the dedicated aero platform into the generalist racing chassis while dropping weight.

While Van Rysel is part of the larger Decathlon organization, the team has historically operated like a much more nimble brand. Part of that agility is evident in the relatively short development cycle we are seeing here. According to the brand, this new platform is the result of a mere two-and-a-half-year turnaround, driven heavily by direct feedback from the Decathlon CMA CGM team.

To land on the final shape, Van Rysel worked through a claimed 13 CFD iterations, five wind-tunnel prototypes, and seven different carbon layups. The stated goal was to find the sweet spot between the aerodynamics of the dedicated RCR-F PRO and the feel of a lightweight climbing bike. To pull that off, the company essentially tried to split the difference across the chassis. By marrying a rigid front end for aerodynamic power transfer with a rear triangle that allows for controlled flex, Van Rysel claims the design mimics the traction and high-speed descending stability of a dedicated climber without sacrificing the speed of an aero rig.

Van Rysel also worked aerodynamic bottles and cages into the overall design. This approach is not unlike what we have seen from Trek and Enve, and the reasoning is obvious: it provides free aero gains with virtually no downside, provided it is executed well. Unfortunately, we won’t know how well it works right away. The images shared only show standard bottles, and Van Rysel notes that “the aero bottles will be released separately from the bikes, with further details to follow.” Despite the delay, the brand claims that in testing featuring turbulence and pedaling legs, the proprietary bottle setup saves up to 6.3 watts at 45 km/h (28 mph) over the previous generation.

Ultimately, both the PRO and the standard model share the exact same silhouette and geometry. They differ only in their carbon fiber layups and component build options, though both frames reportedly utilize the identical 360-gram fork.

At the top of the hierarchy sits the RCR-R PRO. To drop the weight on this tier, Van Rysel relies on a specific blend of super-high-modulus and high-modulus carbon fiber. According to the brand, this layup brings a size medium frame down to 705 grams, making it the lightest chassis the company has ever produced. On the scale, that translates to a claimed complete bike weight of 6.6 kg (14.5 lbs) for the flagship SRAM RED AXS build. For component options, the PRO tier is offered in four configurations: Shimano Dura-Ace Di2, Shimano Ultegra Di2, SRAM RED AXS, and SRAM Force AXS.

Sitting below the flagship model is the standard RCR-R, aimed at riders wanting the new chassis at a more accessible price point. While it uses the same aerodynamic mold as the PRO, Van Rysel relies on a standard high-modulus carbon layup for this tier. That shift in material adds a bit of mass, pushing the claimed frame weight up to 883 grams. On the complete bike side, the Ultegra Di2 build is the lightest configuration offered, tipping the scales at a claimed 7.4 kg (16.3 lbs). To keep costs down, the brand is speccing this frame exclusively with mid-to-upper-tier electronic groupsets, giving buyers the choice of Shimano 105 Di2 or Ultegra Di2, as well as SRAM Rival AXS or Force AXS.

While Van Rysel pulled the cover off the new bikes today at Rouleur Live in London, they won’t be hitting showroom floors immediately. Commercial availability is slated to open after the new year on January 5, 2027. When they do go on sale, European pricing will range from €3,299 up to €8,499 depending on the chosen frame tier and component build. For more details on the new lineup, visit the Van Rysel website .

items.title: Van Rysel announces the new RCR-R Pro bike featuring its lightest ever frame
items.author: thomas.wieckowski@futurenet.com (Tom Wieckowski)
items.content:
Van Rysel has announced two new additions to its range today in the form of new RCR-R Pro and RCR-R models.

The RCR-R Pro is an existing model in the brand's range, but this updated version offers the same frame design in two carbon fibre layup specs and build ranges.

If this news jogs your memory to chatter about Van Rysel prototypes from the summer, you would be right. We first spotted a prototype being raced by Paul Seixas at the Tour Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes back in June.

We also got another good luck at said bike at the Tour de France in July, before Seixas took a thunderous solo win on it at Il Lombardia later in the year.

The time is now seemingly right to unveil the bike officially, coinciding with the bike going on show at Rouleur Live, which takes place in London this weekend.

All bikes will be available to buy from the 5th of January 2027, and Van Rysel says it will be providing a white paper between now and then with more technical details on the bike; here's what we have so far.

Van Rysel has an aero bike in the form of the RCR-F Pro and categorises the RCR-R Pro as a lightweight aerodynamic road bike. The brand says it's been developed to be fast across a range of terrains.

Development has taken place over a span of two and a half years with feedback from the Decathlon CMA CGM team, and as is often the case, the brand says that CFD (computational fluid dynamics), wind tunnel testing, and pro feedback have gone into the development.

Both bike models share the same frame design, but vary in their weights and carbon layups.

The RCR-R Pro uses a mix of super high modulus and high modulus carbon fibre. It weighs a claimed 705 grams for a size medium and is, according to the brand, Van Rysel's lightest ever frame.

The RCR-R frame uses high-modulus carbon and weighs in at a claimed 883 grams for a size medium. The frames both use the same 360-gram fork.

As is the case with most bikes, a blend of features has been sought; Van Rysel says it has looked to combine front-end stiffness with rear-end flex.

Van Rysel tested 13 CFD prototypes, five wind tunnel prototypes and seven frame lay ups before arriving at the bike's final form.

A new aerodynamic water bottle and cage has also been developed, the aero bottles will be released seperately from the bike, but the brand is claiming up to a 6.3 watt saving at 45km/h compared to the previous generation in testing with 'turning legs and turbulence.'

Some WorldTour teams have aero bottles and cages at their disposal but are limited by sponsorship agreements, it remains to be seen whether the team will race with the new components.

Van Rysel says Decathlon CMA CGM riders tested the bike in training and competition this year, with at least Paul Seixas, Nicolas Prodhomme and Matthew Riccitello testing RCR-R PRO prototypes, with Seixas himself saying:

"The bike is lighter, more aerodynamic and, above all, more stable on descents. When you’re travelling at over 100 km/h, confidence in your kit is paramount.

"I clocked up the kilometres in training and worked closely with the Van Rysel engineers to fine-tune the final settings before switching to race mode for the second half of the season. Winning a Monument on this bike is the ultimate validation."

We got a look at one of Seixas' prototypes before the Tour de France kicked off in Barcelona earlier in the year. It was a good chance to take a look at the bike's curved seat tube and profiled stem cover and spacers.

The frame design looks largely the same, but Seixas appeared to ride a raw, unpainted version, which must have saved some extra weight over a painted model.

RCR-R Pro bikes will be available in Shimano Dura-Ace Di2 and Ultegra Di2 builds, as well as SRAM Red and Force.

Complete weights for a medium are a claimed 6.6kg for a SRAM Red build, 6.8kg for a Dura-Ace, and 7.1kg for both Ultegra and Force options.

RCR-R builds will be available in SRAM Force and Rival, as well as Shimano Ultegra and 105 Di2.

Complete weights for a medium are claimed at 7.4 kg for a Shimano Ultegra build, 7.5kg for Force, 7.8kg for 105 and 7.9kg for Rival.

Bikes will range from €3,299 to €8,499, but we don't have any model-specific pricing right now.

items.title: Mike Brown is sticking with Mikal Bridges. For now.
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
In last night’s loss to the Cavaliers, Mikal Bridges played 17 minutes, took three shots, and finished with two points, two rebounds, and an assist. This was another disappointing performance in a season when we expected the wing to make his first All-Star appearance.

At his presser after the game, coach Mike Brown said: “Mikal is a starter, and so it’s not a question of that. He’s like a lot of players. They’ve had their good moments and their not-so-good moments. And Mikal has a proven track record of playing at a pretty high level as a starter in this league. So, for me to make a quote-unquote panic decision and change it right now, we’re ten games in, or whatever we are, I’m not feeling it.”

And in the locker room, Jalen Brunson defended his teammate. “The people in this room have his back night in & night out. We see the work he puts into his game, […] Regardless of what the noise is on the outside, that’s our brother.”

Bridges is an iron man. Between college ball and the pros, he hasn’t missed a game. He’s also one of Jalen Brunson’s closest friends on the team, and as Villanova teammates they won two national titles together. Kal’s mantle is full of pre-pro awards, and he was named to the NBA All-Defensive First Team in 2022. Bridges is a world champion. With a lithe, long body, he’s a tremendous cutter, plays a terrific midrange game, and guards multiple positions well. He’s a career 48% / 37% / 84% shooter, averaging over 14 points and 1.2 steals per game. Maybe not Hall-of-Fame, but definitely Hall-of-Pretty-Good.

In 2024, Brooklyn traded him to New York for a boatload of picks. In just over two seasons at his current home, he’s averaged more than 15 points per game and has been a fixture of the starting lineup.

He’s also been consistently inconsistent. There were times last season when we thought it might be time to sacrifice the games-played streak for a little RnR. After the first five games of the playoffs, we were ready to leave him behind in Atlanta. Then he went on an incredible run, and aside from faltering somewhat against the Spurs, he was essential to New York bringing home a championship. As we know, winning heals a lot of wounds. Those same fans who complained about the overpay soon took up a delirious chant about defiling those picks.

You cannot deny the man’s achievements—nor that he’s stunk so far this season. After a summer of celebration, the 30-year-old has started the current campaign with some of the worst play of his career. Eleven games in, his stats are 5.9 PPG, 33% FG, and 27% 3PT. These Knicks are notoriously late starters, often not hitting their stride until late in the first or even second quarter. Or the fourth. Cap even joked about this in his SNL appearance. But this time, Mikal has no stride to hit. Lately, he has watched the fourth quarter action from the bench (very expensive seats, indeed).

Mike Brown is a supreme diplomat, saying all the right things at all times. Yet, Mikal is a starter because the coach chooses to start him. That’s the coach’s prerogative. The skipper could field someone else as the starting shooting guard—say Landry Shamet, who’s proven himself more than worthy. Why hasn’t he?

First, there’s a chemistry to the team that Mike Brown handles like plutonium. To disrupt the starting five by separating Kal from his ‘Nova brethren might yield positive results on the court, but could foment discord behind the scenes. A demotion could also further erode Bridges’ confidence, which would be bad for their long-term plans. Unless he’s shipped off before the midseason trade deadline (more musings on that below), the Knicks will need Bridges in shape physically and mentally for a deep postseason run.

Further, there’s the potential loss of a reliable sparkplug off the bench. For a while now, Shamet’s been the most consistent in that role. McBride and Clarkson have certainly had their moments, too, but when Mike needs a sub AND a bucket AND defense, ShamWow has become his security blanket. When the score is close, Landry’s steady contribution makes it difficult to justify giving those two-guard minutes to Bridges in the final frame.

Here’s Brown again, from his postgame. “Yeah, part of it is we got two guys that are playing really well in Landry and Deuce, and so it’s hard. [… They] have been a big part of what we’ve done defensively. If they’re playing at a high level, I got to keep trying to find ways to get those guys on the floor.”

As Brown alluded, the Knicks have more guards than they need. Conversely, they remain light at the center position. They have Karl-Anthony Towns playing a career year, Andre Drummond backing him up with great rebounds and questionable shots, and . . . James Wiseman? Sometimes? Leon Rose & Co. are aware of this. They also know that in a trade for a big man of talent, they will need both a desirable player to offer and one whose salary helps to offset what’s incoming.

Obviously, Bridges is a nice guy. He’s not so diabolical as to throw his season to insulate himself from being traded. His sub-standard play does complicate trade opportunities, however. Another club that’s willing to part with a talented center will want to take on a positive, productive player, not a distressed asset with a lot of basketball miles on his wheels.

There’s also a not insignificant chance that the front office is totally cool with what they have and are unwilling to make a panic move either. After all, the team that won the Finals did so with Karl-Anthony Towns, occasional Mitchell Robinson, and a sprinkling of Ariel Hukporti. If Brown can coach Wiseman up to Huk-level participation, then what’s the difference, really?

When asked about his play earlier in this short season, Bridges said, “Obviously we should be better than we are, me personally,” he said. “But it takes time and just not skipping steps.”

He doesn’t sound panicked. Neither does Mike after 11 games. Nor Jalen, Leon, or the rest of the team. What about 15 games? 20? Can we run screaming down the street on December 1st? Ideally, Bridges gets right in Friday’s game against Indy, kills the conversation for the rest of the season, and we all look back and laugh. If this continues to be an issue, though, we’re very interested to see Mike’s next move.

items.title: Hearing set for Audi Tsunoda appeal
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
The FIA has announced that Audi’s appeal against Yuki Tsunoda not getting a penalty at Formula 1’s Italian Grand Prix will be heard on November 25.

Audi complained after the Monza race for what it felt was an incorrect application of the rules against Tsunoda for an alleged grid infringement at the restart.

Tsunoda had been due to line up 14th but, after mistakenly initially heading towards the 15th-place grid slot, he veered at the last-minute to the right-hand side.

While he was able to come to a stop within his intended grid slot, so therefore was not out of position over the front, his Racing Bulls car had ended up at an angle.

That was enough for race director Rui Marques to decide to go for another formation lap because, according to a later stewards' document, "he stated he was not comfortable starting the race with the car in that position".

Tsunoda’s actions had triggered an FIA stewards’ investigation because drivers that cause an extra formation lap are deemed to be in breach of the rules.

Any driver who causes an additional formation lap but is able to start that lap is required to "enter the pitlane at the end of the lap and must start the [session] from the end of the pitlane".

With Tsunoda not serving that, F1's sporting regulations state that any unserved stop-and-go penalty is converted to a 30-second post-race time penalty.

Racing Bulls argued, however, that Tsunoda had not the extra formation lap - as he was still within his grid box and was not impacting any other drivers.

The stewards accepted that position and felt that Tsunoda himself had not been the “cause” of the extra formation lap – which was instead down to Marques’ own choice.

Audi complained, though, as it felt that Tsunoda had indeed been the catalyst for the extra formation lap.

It said in a short statement after Monza that it had "raised a concern regarding the application of Article B5.9.4".

Audi would stand to benefit were Tsunoda to be penalised, because a 30-second sanction would drop him to 15th - with Gabriel Bortoleto being promoted to 10th.

The matter will now be heard at the FIA’s International Court of Appeal in Paris on November 25. The hearing will take place behind closed doors at the request of the FIA, so no public nor media will be allowed to attend.

items.title: Football Daily | ‘The club would like to thank …’: Manchester United dust off the heartfelt exit message
items.author: John Ashdown
items.content:
“Manchester United has announced that David Moyes has left the club. The club would like to place on record its thanks for the hard work, honesty and integrity he brought to the role.”

Oh no! Where will the USA! USA! USA! ever be able to find a manager who could lead us to the dizzying heights of yet another humiliating defeat in the round of 16? A completely empty safari shirt on a clothes hanger could do that. Now he’s leaving the national team to prioritise a club team, which is exactly what he criticised Christian Pulisic for doing a while back. A $10m dollar buyout from Manchester United is a way more appealing prospect than another World Cup cycle with this guy. Adios, Mauricio. I’d add , but for what, exactly?” – Chi.

If any Manchester United fans weren’t already feeling that their board had totally lost its moral compass, then might I suggest that in holding the board meeting to seal Michael Carrick’s fate in Monaco a new bar in tone-deafness has been set. Out of touch, no? . Mauricio, you are going to need it fella. Meanwhile, let’s pencil in the next board meeting for six months’ time or so. Circus Circus in Las Vegas anyone? Might be too many clowns” – John Collins.

With Lil Wayne doing his bit in the jungle, how long before we do actually see Don Pochettino playing a starring role in the Joel & Jim-hosted caper show I’m A Previously Respectable Manager … Get Me Out Of Here?” – Ken Muir.

items.title: Gaia Realini heads for 'new adventure' with Picnic-PostNL, but can climber rejuvenate her career? – Analysis
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Gaia Realini has announced that she's departing Lidl-Trek for a move to Picnic-PostNL next season.

The Italian had spent the past four seasons with Lidl-Trek, with both her and the German team agreeing to end her contract a year early this winter. Now, she's on the move to Dutch squad Picnic-PostNL, she announced in an Instagram post.

"After four years with Lidl-Trek, it's time to start a new chapter. Thank you for all the experiences and moments we shared," Realini wrote.

"I'm happy to announce that I will join Picnic-PostNL for next season, a team that has believed in me from the very beginning and our first conversations.

"New colours, new goals, and plenty of motivation to give my best. Ready for this new adventure!"

After joining Lidl-Trek from Italian squad Isolmant-Premac-Vittoria, Realini had impressed during her first two seasons with the team. She emerged as a top climber, taking podium finishes at the UAE Tour, La Flèche Wallonne, La Vuelta Femenina, and Giro d'Italia in 2023.

Meanwhile, a fifth place at the Tour de France Femmes was her highlight of 2024. She hasn't hit those heights in the past two seasons, however, after suffering a fractured elbow in early 2025.

Her top stage race result of the past two seasons came this September with a 10th-place finish at the Faun Tour Femmes.

Realini is the sixth rider to leave Lidl-Trek for 2027, joining cyclo-cross world champion Lucinda Brand and under-23 world time trial champion Felicity Wilson-Haffenden among notable names on the outgoing list as former Tour de France Femmes champion Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney heads their incoming transfers.

She is, to date, the only confirmed addition for Picnic-PostNL this off-season, while Pfeiffer Georgi, Megan Arens, Rachele Barbieri, and Elise Uijen are on the way out.
