items.title: How Pochettino came on Man Utd's radar - and what Carrick was told when
items.content: <article>How Man Utd identified Mauricio Pochettino as their new head coach - and what happened in the week Michael Carrick was left waiting.</article>
items.lbText:
Michael Carrick must have known what was coming.

Not just because reports of his imminent dismissal were widespread - followed by information about who would be replacing him as Manchester United boss.

But because, effectively, he and his representatives were given heavy enough indications of what was to follow.

On Monday, according to well-placed sources, Carrick's agent was contacted by chief executive Omar Berrada to be told he and director of football Jason Wilcox would be heading to Monaco for a planned meeting with co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe that would include a discussion about the head coach's future.

A day later, it is believed Wilcox had a similar conversation with Carrick.

It is understood that on both occasions it was communicated that a recommendation regarding Carrick's future at the club would be made.

What is not clear is whether Carrick and his representatives knew that recommendation was to relieve him of his duties.

By that point, BBC Sport has been told United were aware of a $10m (£7m) release clause in Mauricio Pochettino's contract with the United States national team. One source even indicated it was representatives of the Argentine who told the Premier League side.

There is some regret behind the scenes at United that machinations leading to Carrick's departure on Thursday were played out so publicly.

But with football clubs the size of United, keeping such developments completely private is extremely difficult - and there is a feeling they were as transparent with Carrick as they could be.

Following heavy defeats by Como and Bournemouth , United placed huge importance on the following three games - against Chelsea, Roma and Aston Villa.

It is understood United's leadership team were clear with Carrick that results and performances needed to improve. A defeat, a victory and draw weren't enough to save him.

There is a feeling that during that three-game period, there was not enough progress, particularly in terms of team structure - underlined by the fact they conceded eight goals.

Pochettino finalising Man Utd deal after Carrick sacking

The chaos that took Carrick from two-year deal to sacked within 15 games

Carrick has conducted himself with great dignity during the turmoil of the past few days and he leaves the club - certainly in the eyes of supporters - with his standing as a United great intact.

When United first appointed Carrick - initially on an interim basis following the sacking of Ruben Amorim in January - he had a positive impact on the squad, and subsequently results.

United liked his positive messaging to the players and media. They felt Carrick brought calm to rocky waters and protected his players at every opportunity - a contrast from at least the closing stages of Amorim's tenure.

On the pitch, the United hierarchy felt Carrick's style of play allowed the forward players more freedom, and they won 12 of their last 17 matches of the season.

While United considered other managerial options in the summer, there was ultimately a sense Carrick had earned a shot at the job on a permanent basis.

The 45-year-old signed a two-year deal, though it is understood United contractually protected themselves in the event of an early termination.

Part of the thought process was to provide the players with some managerial stability given the increased turnover of head coaches in recent years.

Yet the season started poorly with defeat at newly promoted Hull City - and has only spiralled downward since.

United are third bottom of the Premier League and 17th in the Champions League table.

Since Monday, talks have been ongoing with Pochettino.

On Wednesday, Berrada contacted the US Soccer Federation to confirm the existence of the release clause and their intention to activate it.

It is understood the news did not come as a surprise to those across the Atlantic.

Pochettino had been clear with his employers about the discussions with United and - most pertinently - his intention to return to the Premier League.

While United want Pochettino in situ as soon as possible, they are respectful of the fact the USA have two fixtures against Haiti to play - the second of which is on 18 November.

If Pochettino takes charge of the second game, it is understood he will be in place at United's Carrington headquarters on 19 November - four days before they face Liverpool.

items.title: Lindblad and Lawson to continue at Racing Bulls
items.content: <article>Arvid Lindblad and Liam Lawson will continue as the drivers for Red Bull's second team Racing Bulls in 2027.</article>
items.lbText:
Arvid Lindblad and Liam Lawson will continue as the drivers for Red Bull's second team Racing Bulls in 2027.

Red Bull had been deciding whether to promote Bulgarian Formula 2 front-runner Nikola Tsolov in place of Lawson but have decided to spend a second season assessing their current line-up

Tsolov will be the reserve driver for both teams next season.

Team principal Alan Permane said: "I have no doubt that this is the best driver line-up for us, bringing a strong combination of experience and ambition.

"Both have demonstrated their ability and potential throughout the season, and we've seen the progress they've made, both individually and as a pairing."

The decision to retain both marks a break from the previous Red Bull philosophy of fast-tracking drivers through the programme.

Chequered Flag Extra: The Making of Kimi Antonelli

Racing Bulls essentially exists to find potential drivers for the main Red Bull team, so the company has tended to jettison drivers who have been given a chance and not succeeded.

That's why Lawson, 24, was considered vulnerable. He was promoted to Red Bull alongside Max Verstappen for the 2025 season only to be demoted after just two races in which he had struggled.

The New Zealander has since sought to rebuild his career and was much more convincing when he was re-promoted to Red Bull for the Dutch, Italian and Spanish Grands Prix this year while regular driver Isack Hadjar was recovering from a broken wrist.

Keeping Lawson on board for 2027 gives Red Bull a known-quality benchmark with which to continue their assessment of Lindblad, who made his debut this season.

The 19-year-old Briton has excelled at times in his rookie year but on average has been a little behind Lawson, who has out-qualified him 13 times to nine and has scored more than twice as many points.

Lawson said: "We've had a brilliant season together and the team has worked very hard to produce a fast car, which I've loved driving.

"It feels great to be part of a historic season for the team as we continue our fight for fifth place in the constructors' championship.

"I'm looking forward to carrying this moment forward with Arvid through to 2027; we're building something super positive and I'm excited by what we can achieve together."

Lindblad added: "It's been a truly special year, full of new experiences and learnings since the very first pre-season test. I'd like to thank everyone for their trust and support.

"I can't wait to get started next year, building on everything I've learned during my rookie season."

The news release announcing the pairing made no mention of Tsolov, who is expected to be retained by Red Bull in some form of reserve role in which he gains experience through work in the simulator and with testing previous cars.

items.title: Yankees Birthday of the Day: Carl Mays
items.author: Andrew Mearns
items.content:
Carl Mays probably would’ve enjoyed one single entry in the annals of baseball lore that doesn’t mention the most regrettable of the thousands of pitches that he threw across a 15-year career that saw him capture four World Series titles. Alas, even on his 135th birthday, we cannot grant that wish. No matter how great he was on the mound, his story will always be tied to that of Cleveland shortstop Ray Chapman. That’s just how it is.

November 12, 1891 (Liberty, KY) April 4, 1971 (El Cajon, CA): 1919-23

Mays was born in Kentucky to a Methodist minister named William Mays (ah, baseball coincidences), who died when Carl was just 12 years old. The family had moved to Missouri by then, but they packed up again after William’s death, en route to Kingfisher, Oklahoma. It was a sad time for Mays’ family, but he did get the opportunity to meet his cousin, John Long. He was a catcher, and he introduced Mays to the game. Pitching to Long, Mays developed the raw skills to attract the notice of traveling teams.

At the age of 20, Mays signed with the Class D Western Tri-State League’s Boise Irrigators, who offered him $90 per month. Mays was certainly worth the deal, as he pitched to a 2.08 ERA, 0.930 WHIP, and a 22-9 record in 280.2 innings. He moved up to the Class B team in Portland and again had a fine season, though won/loss record (10-15) deceived his true performance (2.45 ERA, 1.024 WHIP in 250 innings), and it was enough to get a new contract for 1914 with the Providence Grays, a Rhode Island team owned by the Detroit Tigers.

The Boston Red Sox purchased the Grays from the Tigers during the season, and Mays attracted Boston’s interested with a fantastic season: 24-8 and a 2.57 ERA in 273.1 innings. Another young pitcher joined him down the stretch named Babe Ruth, and their pitching helped Providence win the pennant. By the beginning of next season, Mays was a major-league pitcher.

The submariner worked mostly out of the bullpen in his rookie season, appearing in 38 games but 131.2 innings overall of 90 ERA- and 69 FIP- ball. He threw hard and was not at all afraid to throw high and inside to back hitters off the plate. Even as a rookie, he made an enemy of Ty Cobb, whose own nasty attitude clashed with Mays. On one occasion, Cobb was knocked down and then dragged a bunt up the first base line, where he spiked Mays with his sharp cleats and cut his leg. Boston and Detroit fought hard for the pennant in 1915; a 100-win season was not good enough to win the title for Detroit. Boston beat the Phillies in five games for the 1915 World Series title, but while he was a champion in his first season, Mays did not appear in any of the games.

The next couple seasons saw Mays slowly transition from splitting time more evenly between the ‘pen and rotation to becoming an established rotation presence and the ace of a championship staff. Although he was a bit of a loner, there was no denying his competitiveness on the mound. The Red Sox repeated as champions in 1916, and Mays had his best year in Boston in 1917, pitching to a 1.74 ERA (69 ERA-) in 289 innings while also unsurprisingly leading the league in hit by pitches. Only two pitchers in baseball had a better ERA than Mays that year and despite the HBPs, he had a 1.052 WHIP. His pitches simply sank, and many batters could not do any better than hitting it on the ground while hoping it found a hole in the infield:

Yankees infielder Roger Peckinpaugh said Mays threw “a very ‘heavy’ ball. It sinks and when you catch it, it feels heavy enough to almost go through your glove.” Horace Ford, who batted against Mays in the National League, said that hitting Mays’s fastball “was like hitting a chuck of lead. It would go clunk and you’d beat it into the ground.”– Allan Wood, SABR

Boston finished nine games behind the White Sox for the AL pennant that year, but another fine season by Mays in 1918 brought them back on top. While his ERA and ERA- jumped a bit to 2.21 and 84, respectively, his WHIP was almost identical and he led the league in both shutouts (8) and complete games (30). Those marks were made more impressive by the fact that the season ended early after 126 games on September 2nd due to World War I. The Red Sox played the Cubs in the Fall Classic, and Mays received the ball in Game 3 with the series tied at one game apiece. He beat the Cubs 2-1, going the distance with just one walk allowed, scattering seven hits. Boston and Chicago split the next two games, so Mays got the start in Game 6 to close out the Cubbies, and he did just that by spinning a three-hitter in another 2-1 victory. Mays was the last man to throw a pitch for a championship Red Sox team in the next 86 years.

Although his teammates were not fond of Mays for his somewhat antisocial personality and irritance on the mound when they committed errors, it seemed as though Boston and Mays had a fine relationship. It all came to a sudden halt in 1919. Boston struggled to give him much run support, and Mays became highly frustrated with the offense. From a personal standpoint, his Missouri home had burned down, and he grew so annoyed with the Philadelphia fans during one series that he hurled a baseball from the dugout at a fan. Finally, in a July 13th game against the White Sox, catcher Wally Schang clocked him in the head with a throw on a stolen base by Eddie Collins.

Soon afterward, manager and future Yankees GM Ed Barrow removed him from the game, and he stormed off the field, chucking the ball against the backstop. Mays was suspended by the Red Sox and told sportswriters that he demanded a trade. Soon, owner Harry Frazee obliged, sending Mays to the Yankees on July 29th in exchange for two unremarkable pitchers and $40,000.

“Carl, this is [co-owner] Cap Huston of the Yankees. I called to find out if you would be interested in pitching for the Yankees. If you are, there’s a good chance of my swinging a deal for you tonight, but I didn’t want to get all tangled up in negotiations if you wouldn’t pitch for us.”“Well, how about the money?”

“We’ll have no problems there. Just pack your bag, and by the time you get here, we’ll be ready to talk contract.”

– excerpted from Marty Appel’s “Pinstripe Empire”

AL president Ban Johnson was furious about the trade since a suspended player was dealt and essentially controlled his own fate over the authority of the Red Sox owner. The reserve clause was supposed to bind a player to his team without much control over it, but Mays worked around the system. He demanded that the trade be voided and that Mays be returned to Boston, but Yankee owners Jacob Ruppert and Cap Huston flat-out refused and told Johnson that if necessary, they would go to court to keep Mays on the Yankees. New York State Supreme Court Justice Robert F. Wagner granted a temporary injunction allowing Mays to pitch for the Yankees.

Johnson’s decision was rendered meaningless, and Mays made 13 starts for the Yankees down the stretch as the team bid to pass the infamous “Black Sox” in the AL pennant race. Although the White Sox ended up running away with the pennant as the Yankees finished in third place with an 80-59 record, it was not Mays’ fault by any means. He was outstanding, pitching to a 1.65 ERA and 51 ERA-, winning nine of his starts, completing all but one of them, and throwing a shutout as well. In just 13 starts, he was worth 2.6 rWAR and 2.2 fWAR for a rising Yankees team. They had their ace, and now they needed a hitting star. They enlisted Mays’ former rotationmate Ruth, who was a pretty fair hitter.

With Mays and Ruth in tow, the Yankees had a superb team ready for the 1920 campaign. They finished the year with a then-franchise record 95 wins and a .617 winning percentage, though they ended up behind pennant-winning Cleveland by two games. The race between the two teams was sadly marred by tragedy in a game on August 16th at the Yankees’ home, the Polo Grounds.

Mays was in the midst of another fine season, wherein he led the league with six shutouts, pitched 312 innings, and ended with a 3.06 ERA (81 ERA-). The unpopular Mays faced perhaps his polar opposite at the plate leading off the fifth inning in beloved Cleveland shortstop Ray Chapman, a perennially fantastic player who had already amassed a 28.9 fWAR career in just nine years and 1,051 games with Cleveland. He was only 29, a potential Hall of Famer in the making. Even Cobb liked him. However, Chapman had a tendency to lean over the plate, and Mays threw an inside fastball toward him to start this at-bat. What happened next was unclear: either Chapman ducked unfortunately right into the ball’s path attempting a drag bunt, or he never moved at all. Either way, it got him square in the temple with a sickeningly loud crack.

It struck Chapman so hard that the ball caromed back toward the mound, and Mays’ immediate action was to throw the ball to first base in case it hit Chapman’s bat. Chapman’s teammates helped him off the field, as he was still conscious. They brought him to St. Lawrence Hospital, where he was diagnosed with a fractured skull and died the next day, the only player to ever die as the result of a pitch in an MLB game.

“It was the most regrettable incident of my career, and I would give anything if I could undo what has happened.“– Carl Mays

The whole incident was a horrible experience for everyone involved; Mays was contrite but overall did not handle it particularly well, noting that there was scuff on the ball (which he always normally liked to do anyway), and that he didn’t expect Chapman to duck into the ball. He insisted to his dying day that he did not throw at Chapman. Regardless, the tragedy only emphasized the reason why baseball banned the spitball at the beginning of the year, with only those who already threw it allowed to use it via grandfather clause. Strangely, it still took over 35 years before players started wearing helmets in the batter’s box.

Mays became synonymous with Chapman’s death, and while he pitched another nine years in The Show, most people only remember Mays for that tragic pitch. Mays’ best season in New York actually occurred the very next year. He did what he could to put the incident behind him and paced the league with 27 wins, 49 games (38 starts), and a career-high 336.2 innings pitched. He was brilliant in a 4.5-fWAR campaign, and the Bombers outlasted Cleveland to win their first pennant in franchise history. Mays completed nine of his ten starts down the stretch and even tossed in a relief appearance; the Yankees won all but one of those games.

In the first game of the unusual best-of-nine, all-Polo Grounds World Series against John McGraw’s Giants, Mays put the Yankees ahead with a dominant five-hit shutout. He didn’t walk anyone, and only two batters made it past first base. The teams split the next two games, and Mays had the chance to give the Yankees a 3-1 series lead in Game 4, but Phil Douglas outpitched him. Mays held a slim 1-0 lead into the top of the eighth, but an Irish Meusel triple, singles by Johnny Rawlings and Fred Snyder, and a two-run double by George Burns gave the Giants three runs. The Yankees lost 4-2 to even the series.

Manager Miller Huggins turned back to Mays on just two days’ rest in Game 7 with the series even at 3-3. The only other starter in the pitching well was Waite Hoyt, so the Yankees were desperate. Mays did just about all he could do, allowing just six hits to the Giants, but a two-out double by Snyder in the seventh scored Rawlings, who reached on an error by second baseman Aaron Ward. Again, the Yankees were unable to do much against Douglas, and they lost 2-1. The Giants finished off the series five games to three on the strength of a 1-0 four-hit shutout by Art Nehf against Hoyt. There was some talk that Mays fixed the game in the two losses, but that was never proven and seems highly risky and unlikely given the then-recent lifetime bans suffered by the “Black Sox” players who threw the 1919 World Series. The Giants were just a damn good team, and they beat one of the best pitchers in baseball during the tiring late innings of two games.

With almost 2,000 regular season and playoff innings on Mays’ arm in seven seasons, he began to decline somewhat at age 30 in 1922. He was still a solid pitcher with a 3.60 ERA and a 90 ERA-, but he was never as dominant as he was in ‘21 ever again. The Yankees won their second straight pennant in ’22 and again faced McGraw’s Giants in the World Series. This time, it was not nearly as close. The series returned to a best-of-seven and the Giants won Games 1 and 3 to take a 2-0 lead (Game 2 ended in a 3-3 tie called on account of darkness). Mays got the nod in Game 4, but despite getting staked to an early two-run advantage, a four-run fifth led to a 4-3 loss. The Giants finished off their undefeated series with a 5-3 victory in Game 5, as Nehf finished off the Yankees for the second straight year.

The Yankees had grown weary of Mays by 1923, and they reportedly sought to trade him before the season. Nothing happened though, so Huggins just barely used him throughout the Yankees’ pennant three-peat. Mays pitched poorly when he did appear, so it was not as though the Yankees were squandering anyone valuable. He did not appear in the Fall Classic of the Yankees’ first championship, as they finally beat the Giants.

The Cincinnati Reds bought Mays from the Yankees after the ’23 campaign, and he managed to stick around with them for five more years, alternating between healthy and injury-plagued seasons. He had a comeback season at age 34 in ’26, leading the NL with 24 complete games and pitching to a 3.14 ERA (85 ERA-) in 281 innings, a 4.7 fWAR season. The Reds finished just two games behind the Cardinals for the NL pennant. Exhausted, Mays pitched just 144.2 innings over his next two years with the Reds, and finished his MLB career with one mediocre season on McGraw’s Giants as the decade came to a close.

Mays pitched two years in the minor league American Association and Pacific Coast League, then officially ended his playing career at age 40. His baseball career did not fully conclude though; he had made amends with the Cleveland organization and scouted for them, Milwaukee, and Kansas City over the next 20 years. He lived until he was 79 years old, passing away in ‘71 with the game a whole lot different than it was when he began. Mays was a crucial member of the first Yankee teams of any sustained success, and his contributions to those teams should not be forgotten.

See more of the “Yankees Birthday of the Day” series here.

items.title: Matthew Richardson Allegedly Targeted Teammate With Offensive Images in Track Worlds Scandal
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Richardson sent home from Shanghai in disgrace after reportedly using homophobic and racist slurs as British Cycling is rocked by allegations of 'toxic culture.'
items.lbText:
(Photo: Dilara Irem Sancar/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Matthew Richardson was sent home from the UCI track world championships last month in disgrace after he allegedly targeted a teammate with offensive images.

That’s the new detail The Times reported Tuesday on a scandal that’s rocked the small world of track cycling.

The Times wrote that Richardson – one of the best sprinters of his era – had left a long regular trail of homophobic and discriminatory remarks about people from minority backgrounds.

One of those was made in a message that included “a deeply offensive image with reference to another Team GB rider.”

The image sparked an allegation being made against Richardson.

The complaint saw him sent home from Shanghai by British Cycling on the eve of October’s UCI track worlds.

“The Times has seen extensive evidence, dating back over a number of years, of images and messages sent by Richardson to other riders. He appears to make discriminatory remarks about people from minority backgrounds on a regular basis,” reads the report.

“The Times has seen six different messages where he appears to use the racially offensive n-word, and others where he jokes about his use of that word. He also appears to have made a number of offensive references to the Asian community and homophobic comments. Another senior source claims to have seen a separate image, again sent to riders, that references a rider from another international team and uses the n-word.”

Richardson was born in England but moved to Australia as a child.

He switched racing nationality from Australian to English in 2024.

British Cycling confirmed it opened an investigation into Richardson’s conduct after he was axed from its world championship squad.

The 27-year-old vowed he would fully co-operate in the proceedings “with contrition.”

However, according to The Times, the allegations against Richardson dated back to July – three months before the investigation was opened. Additionally, Richardson was only withdrawn 48 hours before the world championships in Shanghai last month.

These developments come at a difficult time for British Cycling.

In a separate thread, The Times reported that an independent feedback survey of the federation uncovered a drop in morale among elite riders, a lack of accountability in senior leadership, and accusations of a “toxic culture.”

Richardson’s agent has distanced himself from the rider in the wake of the allegations against the rider.

However, Richardson is still headlining the London 3-Day track cycling event this weekend. The event is not affiliated to British Cycling.

British Cycling has not provided any timelines on the conclusion of its investigation.

items.title: Netcompany Ineos end long-term partnership with Continental to switch to Pirelli tyres for 2027
items.author: thomas.wieckowski@futurenet.com (Tom Wieckowski)
items.content:
Netcompany Ineos will race on Pirelli tyres from 2027 onwards, bringing an end to a a long-term partnership with Continental.

Launching as Sky Procycling in 2010, the British team used a range of tyres from manufacturers like Veloflex, FMB, and Vittoria in their early years, but have consistently used Continental for more than a decade now.

However, a new three-year agreement with Pirelli was. announced on Thursday.

"Pirelli bring a huge amount of technical expertise and a real commitment to innovation, so it's exciting to have them working closely with our riders and performance team," said the team's Director of Racing, Geraint Thomas.

"It's not just about the equipment we race on, but how we can work together to keep developing, so we're really looking forward to building that relationship and seeing what we can achieve together."

Netcompany Ineos will make their racing debut on Pirelli rubber at the Santos Tour Down Under in January.

'Marginal gains' is still a phrase that's closely linked to Netcompany Ineos, and there is some mention of that philosophy in the Pirelli press release.

Pirelli says the partnership will focus on developing 'technical solutions' to the demands of WorldTour cycling. There's also a mention of 'technical assessment' being a key step in the development of the partnership.

In simple language, this could point to the team testing the Pirelli tyres against the Continental GP 5000 S TR and TT TR tyres they have been racing on until now.

Pirelli already supplies two WorldTour teams: Lidl-Trek and Alpecin-Premier Tech.

It sounds like Netcompany Ineos will primarily use the Pirelli P Zero Race SL-R tyre as well as the P Zero Race RS model.

The team also switched wheels at the start of this year, moving from Shimano Dura-Ace wheels to Scope models. Perhaps the Scope wheels and Pirelli tyre combination has proven to be faster.

We tested road tyres in our CN Labs tyre test in 2024, testing both Continental and Pirelli models, but that test didn't include the then unreleased P Zero Race SL-R.

Pirelli launched its flagship P Zero Race SL-R tyre in March this year. The tyres use PAAS (Pirelli Advanced Aerodynamic System technology), which adds material to the sidewalls of the slick tyre to improve aerodynamic performance when mounted to a rim. Pirelli claimed rolling resistance and aero performance had improved considerably compared to its P Zero RACE RS model.

The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. Subscribe for unlimited access to our comprehensive news coverage, industry-leading CN Labs testing, expert columnists, and so much more. Plus, the Cyclingnews app means you can stay up-to-date wherever you go!

items.title: Factor Bikes strengthens its partnership with Team Amani with three-year title sponsorship deal
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
After recently announcing that it will support Bahrain Victorious for 2027 and beyond, Factor Bikes is extending its presence in the pro peloton by becoming a title sponsor for Team Amani.

The team will be known as Team Amani Factor Racing from 2027 until the end of 2029, with Factor’s founder, Rob Gitelis, convinced the team can reach the highest levels of the women’s sport.

Factor and Amani have worked together for four years, but the new deal will not only include the bike brand in the team’s name, but also bring the team into Factor's performance programme, as they do with their other pro teams. As such, they will ride the company’s Ostro VAM and Ostro Gravel frames rolling on Black Inc wheels.

The partnership will include not only the Women’s Continental road team, but also their off-road programme and the Black Mamba Development squad.

Amani is a proudly African team, competing with a roster comprised entirely of women from the continent. While they’ve been around as a club-level team for a few years, they graduated to UCI level only at the start of the 2026 season.

During that time, they took three wins, all at fourth-tier .2 level races in Africa, though they showed real promise on European roads, especially at the Volta Ciclista Catalunya, where Haftu Eyerusalem Reda finished 20th in the general classification in the mountainous three-day race.

Despite their status as one of the youngest teams in the bunch, Amani have stated their ambition to ride the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift in 2028. However, with UCI Regulations as they currently are, achieving that is likely to require the team to shift up a level from Women’s Continental to ProTeam to guarantee a start at the biggest race on the calendar.

"Of everything we’re doing in racing, Amani is the project I feel most personally invested in," Gitelis said. "We’re back in the men’s WorldTour and expanding our racing programme, which is exciting, but I want to devote real time and resources to this over the next three years. I believe this team can compete at the sharp end of the women’s WorldTour with the right support, experience and time.

"Beyond racing, I believe the opportunities that it creates can change the lives of the women involved. That’s why Amani belongs within Factor Racing."

Mikel Delagrange, Amani’s founder, welcomed Factor’s extended commitment, saying: "What has impressed me most about Factor is that when they say they’re going to do something, they do it. Every commitment they’ve made to this team over the past four years has been planned carefully and delivered in full.

"That’s rare in this world, and it’s exactly what a team like ours needs. Taking on title sponsorship is the biggest step yet, and I trust it completely because I’ve seen how Factor works. We have a clear goal for 2028, and the right partner to help us get there."

items.title: Tsolov gets twin F1 2027 reserve role to prepare him for race seat
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Red Bull has named Nikola Tsolov the official reserve driver of both of its Formula 1 teams in 2027 with a programme “designed to ensure he is fully prepared to race in F1 at the highest level”.

Tsolov missed out on a 2027 Racing Bulls seat as Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad were both handed extensions into next year. 

But Red Bull has made clear Tsolov is still very much the next driver in line for an F1 seat, confirming on the same day Lawson and Lindblad were confirmed for 2027 that Tsolov would be made reserve. 

Tsolov is currently fighting for the Formula 2 title with 2027 Haas F1 driver Rafael Camara and Alex Dunne, having taken six race wins with two rounds in Qatar and Abu Dhabi remaining. 

Tsolov finished runner-up to Camara in his third Formula 3 campaign last year. 

Red Bull's announcement read: “In his new role, Nikola will undertake an extensive development programme, combining simulator and development work with valuable track experience through Free Practice sessions, Testing of Previous Cars (TPC), selected test sessions and tyre testing. 

“Alongside his responsibilities as a reserve driver, the programme is designed to ensure he is fully prepared to race in F1 at the highest level.” 

Tsolov said he was “incredibly happy and grateful” to Red Bull for the opportunity. 

“My ambition is clear: I want to become an F1 driver,” he said.

“Having the opportunity to spend next year preparing for that next step is incredibly exciting. I’m confident that with the team’s support and experience, I’ll have the best possible preparation to make sure I’m fully ready to take the next step onto the F1 grid when the time comes.” 

Tsolov impressed Racing Bulls with his FP1 debut in Mexico where he compared favourably to 2026 rookie Lindblad. 

“Nikola is an exceptionally talented young driver, and we have been hugely impressed by his development and performances over the past few years,” Red Bull team boss Laurent Mekies said.

“To fight for the championship in F3 and now challenge for the F2 title in his first full season says a great deal about his ability and determination. 

“What has impressed us just as much is his maturity, his approach to racing and his willingness to keep learning and improving.

“We have enormous belief in Nikola’s potential and see him as a driver with a very exciting future in F1. 

“This appointment reflects our confidence in him and our commitment to his continued development. Our focus in 2027 will be on giving him the experience, tools and support he needs to be ready to race in F1 next.”

items.title: Tsolov lands reserve driver role for F1 2027
PHD chemistry and three types of sand – Inside the CeramicSpeed chain lubricant test labs
items.author: thomas.wieckowski@futurenet.com (Tom Wieckowski)
items.content:
Cyclists have been applying lubricants to their bicycle chains for well over a century. From the invention of 3-in-1 oil in 1894 to condition-specific wet and dry formulations, through to hot waxing and the performance-focused, watt-saving lubricants we have today.

There are now countless products promising an increase in speed, quietness and longevity. Currently, no industry-standard test procedures exist for chain lubricants and waxes, and what is the best thing to test? There are established big names, but how can you tell an effective product from one that might actually do your drivetrain harm?

CeramicSpeed is one brand that formulates and tests all of its own chain waxes and lubricants in-house. A fact which possibly draws less attention than the brand's more visible high-end ceramic bearings and OSPW pulley wheel systems.

I visited the CeramicSpeed headquarters in Holstebro, Denmark, where the brand has dedicated chain-lubricant formulation and test labs in an attempt to answer a few of the questions the chain lube nerd in me had, and to learn more about how you go about formulating an effective chain lubricant or wax, testing it and bringing it to market.

The origins of the modern-day chain waxing revolution lie with Jason Smith’s Friction Facts chain lubricant and testing business, which carried out some of the very first, if not the first, dedicated drivetrain friction testing over a decade ago.

CeramicSpeed acquired FrictionFacts in 2016, including at least one of its test machines, and then built on Smith’s original UFO product foundation. Smith joined the business as well, and later worked on the Driven chainless drivetrain project, but is no longer involved.

Product development and rigorous testing are a cornerstone of the CeramicSpeed product philosophy. The brand commits plenty of time to formulating and testing chain products.

Various brands carry out their own lubricant testing; some do none. It varies, and more than one brand markets its products as the fastest. ZeroFriction, an Australian independent testing company, is a reference point for many who are interested in lubricants and testing, but a lot happens behind closed doors.

CeramicSpeed chain products begin life in the brand's lab. Glass flasks line a wall, and at the end of a workbench topped with several machines that look a bit like microscopes, there’s a cabinet full of the base ingredients used to produce chain lubes and wax. This being Denmark early in the year, the carpet of snow on the ground outside matches the colour of the product in some of the bottles today.

Lina Søbjerg Madsen, a PHD chemist, and Michael Pedersen, Development Engineer, have both been with CeramicSpeed for the best part of a decade and form the backbone of the brand's wax and lubricant development and testing programme. If you have used a CeramicSpeed lube or wax product in that time, they will have developed and tested it.

CeramicSpeed wax and lube products are both wax-based. Hot melt wax is a blend of pure waxes, including what Søbjerg Madsen tells me, with a grin, is her 'secret ingredient'.

When it comes to a drip chain lubricant in a bottle, Ceramicspeed uses wax, emulsifiers, a corrosion inhibitor to protect the chain, which it claims not every brand uses, and demineralised water as the carrier, which is what, as the name suggests, helps carry the wax lubricant itself deep into your chain links, where it can do its work and protect the chain.

Drip lubricants are mixed thoroughly using machines, heated, and then cooled. Today's formulations are water-based, but the original carrier fluid for the first UFO Drip was kerosene, which was known to melt bottle nozzles over time due to its aggressive nature.

The water-based carrier evaporates, leaving behind the wax. Oil-based drip lubricants tend to become dirtier in use because contamination is suspended within the oil, which remains on the chain.

Charged with developing CeramicSpeed’s chain lube offerings, Søbjerg Madsen begins by explaining that it’s not possible to have one product that’s the best at everything.

“What people need to understand is that there are over 1000 different waxes; there are synthetic and natural products, and each of them has different properties. She explains.

“So when sales suggests a new lubricant or a new product, my main goal is to ask, 'What kind of properties do you want?’, because you can't have everything.

“The first part is getting the wax composition with the properties that I would like, and once that's done, then I need to find a way to keep it in this water solution, and also get the shelf life correct, and that's a really difficult task.” Søbjerg Madsen explains.

A product's composition depends on the desired properties. Is longevity the priority, or is all-out efficiency the goal? Something that lasts for a thousand kilometres may very well not be the fastest option.

CeramicSpeed's approach is that a one-size-fits-all product isn't ideal for chain treatments. The first wet lube, for instance, went through 300 experiments to arrive at the desired composition.

Cyclists, or at least road cyclists with a focus on performance, often look for what's fastest, or what saves watts, but there's more to it than that. Making a quality product that performs for the most amount of riders, across different regions, climates and weather systems is a tricky ask.

CeramicSpeed offers three drip products: All Conditions, Wet, and Indoor and the range was overhauled this year and given a new look.

All Conditions and Speed Wax are the best bet for speed; Wet lasts longer and protects your chain in the rain, and Indoor doesn't shed like a regular wax, making it useful for the velodrome or home training. The new Ultra Endurance Wax doesn't focus on low friction, a first for the brand; its priority is high durability and consistent performance over hundreds of kilometres.

It is 'stickier'. It might not be the quickest option for a road race, but it will protect a chain for hundreds of kilometres off-road in a gravel race, for example. A super-fast chain wax or lube's benefits will be null and void if it's gone after 2 hours of hard use.

The brand's chain lubricants are developed in small batches in the lab and produced in volumes of up to two litres. These samples are used for the brand's testing and by test riders.

The brand now also has an in-house production facility where it can produce 50- 300 kg of drip product in a batch, allowing them to control the process.

Søbjerg Madsen explains that this close proximity means it can be easy to address issues that may arise from production at scale.

“Sometimes, because it's chemistry, and chemistry can be unpredictable when you scale up, we'll see some issues where I have to correct something, then when they say go, they are ready to produce and put it in bottles,” she explains.

Shelf life is another factor when it comes to our chain lubricant; top tip: don’t leave the cap off your water-based drip chain wax, as the water will evaporate over time.

CeramicSpeed aims for a two-year product shelf life, and needs to ensure a product doesn't solidify in the bottle. Søbjerg Madsen explains that a drip lube which separates in the bottle is a poor sign, something to look for when you are next in the bike shop buying chain lube.

"That's a very poor sign; it's a sign that it's unstable, and the product development didn't do a good enough job.

"Every time I make the sample, I put it in the incubator at 40 degrees. It stays there for three months, and if it doesn't solidify or separate, then we say we have a shelf life of two years," she says.

After nearly a decade, it's clear the pair have a strong feel for what's needed, but verification from the test lab's machines and Pedersen's experience and feel inform the direction Søbjerg Madsen needs to take at times.

"When I make the first wax compositions, and I think 'Okay, this might be interesting,' then I'll make a test chain for Michael and ask him to do an experiment to measure the watts, because then I have an idea. If it's really high, then I need to do something to make it lower," she explains.

The testing lab and three different kinds of sand

The lubricant and wax formulations are designed, and then the testing phase takes around six months on average, though the brand is always busy testing different things, including the competition, and running experiments.

Engineer Pedersen has tested a lot of products in general in the lab, including over 800 chains; the 11-speed Shimano Dura-Ace chain is held in particularly high regard. If you are running 11-speed Shimano, buy yourself a Dura-Ace chain.

CeramicSpeed uses a combination of internal and external test riders. This includes company founder and CEO Jacob Csizmadia himself; we pass a few of his stealth all-black bikes in the corridor on our way to the lab.

The test lab is a fairly small, brightly lit room that is lined with workbenches. Many of which are topped with testing machines, which in different ways all vaguely resemble a bicycle drivetrain.

There are five chain testing machines, which all serve a different purpose; There's the original Friction Facts testing machine, a clean conditions test machine, a wet conditions test machine, a machine to add water and sand contaminants together and the brand's latest baby, the Full Load Watt Tester machine (FLWT); a larger unit, which runs as a complete drivetrain, whilst adding sand and water and measuring friction. This machine has been designed to take the brand's testing to the next level.

CeramicSpeed measures friction in watts by using torque sensors. The durability of the chain treatment is also monitored, but chain wear specifically is not, though it can be as part of a specific extra-long extreme test.

The Friction Facts test machine was the original, weighting a single-speed arrangement at 250 watts of load in a clean environment. It's a style of machine being used by other brands to test as well, but it isn't a full drivetrain and can skew results because the chain is in tension pretty much the whole time due to there being no derailleur.

A Tribology test for friction rates called a Pin and Disc test also exists, and whilst it can be performed to an ISO standard, it isn't specific to bicycle drivetrains or modern wax formulas. CeramicSpeed don't consider it to be a worthwhile testing avenue to go down.

For years, only clean-conditions testing could be done, but as Søbjerg Madsen points out, unless you are riding in a velodrome environment, "we all know even on a hot summer day, it's not completely clean conditions," meaning dust and other contaminants are still present.

A machine that could add contamination was required to mimic real-world conditions. The wet conditions test machine was also developed, but adding only water could only tell so much.

"We could only add water, and a lot of water, and what does that really simulate in the real world?" Søbjerg Madsen says. Every cyclist knows a wet, rainy day comes with all sorts of grit, dirt, and mud that also interact with a chain.

CeramicSpeed has now developed a machine capable of adding contamination and water. The FLWT machine is run using four different protocols that simulate different conditions over five hours; to standardise things, because, as the pair point out, you could end up just testing forever.

These test protocols are as follows:

- Clean test without contamination.- Tests with water added every five minutes. - Dry test with sand added every five minutes.- Extreme test with water and sand added every 15 minutes.

The brand also uses three different types of sand from around the world in testing because, naturally, it varies all over the world. Sand from Australia, Denmark and America is used. The sands all differ; the one from Colorado in the US is very fine and dusty, the sample from Australia has more clay, and the Danish sand has more 'fine particles'; using it consistently allows for repeatable testing.

The FLWT machine uses a motor to power a drivetrain at a load of 250 watts (though this can be altered) and advanced torque sensors on the input and output axles to measure the wattage difference; custom test software has also been written in-house to calculate the test results.

CeramicSpeed runs various tests, and the brand was careful not to give me everything; it's a competitive area, so we couldn't dive into all of the test data, graphs and findings. The brand has published some test results on its site for its chain lubricants.

Generally, though, tests last five hours, and multiple runs of each test are completed for validation. When test graphs are produced, they show a break in time, an optimal running period and a decline in performance due to wear and/or abrasion from the test contaminants.

The FLWT can also be remotely controlled and has a built-in horn to warn colleagues that a test is about to start when the engineers are working remotely.

There is even a microphone to monitor the changing sound of a chain's treatment as testing progresses and a lubricant 'wears in'. The sound a chain is making can tell the engineers a lot, and plenty of riders recognise a change in sound as a reminder to re-lube or re-wax their chains.

Apparatus in workshops to break in freshly waxed chains is also getting more complex; the brand's advice: re-install your freshly waxed chain, work it by hand a little if needed and go ride it; it will settle down and go quiet soon enough.

"We know from the industry that there are a lot of people who are looking into this (an FLWT-style machine), but we have also realised that the problem is getting reproducible data. says Søbjerg Madsen.

"We really need to be sure that what we are measuring is correct,"

The team admit that they are still learning the machine, and are aiming to measure very fine differences consistently in order to be as accurate as possible, in part because differences between competitor products are very small.

No lubricant test standard exists in the bike industry, and you can't really just go and buy a test machine. This means brands are free to present their testing in whichever way suits them best.

"Customers and the companies are saying, 'Well, of course, you're just designing your test to make yours look best,' and that's what everybody is doing, because there is no standard.

"That's what everybody is doing; they are making their own test, and then, of course, they look best, but what Michael and I are really doing, and it's easy for us to say, is that we are really trying to make tests that mimic the real world. It's much easier to optimise something if you have a standard test to do it," says Søbjerg Madsen

The brand is comparing against the competition, but appears to be doing it fairly, setting up and testing competitor products to spec, as Søbjerg Madsen explains.

"If we're doing comparison tests on one of our competitors, we do a lot of work to test it at what they recommend.

"We are not just trying to make it look awful. Sometimes we find that, well, this lubricant is actually really good under these conditions, and then, of course, as a chemist and scientist, I'm thinking, 'okay, what do they do that's really good, and how can I optimise mine to get the same performance?"

The clue is in the name: with CeramicSpeed, the brand is all about speed and low friction; however, its efforts with chain treatments, drip and hot wax go beyond being able to say 'ours is fastest'. It's a statement the engineers do not make themselves during my visit.

Cyclists can make an informed decision on what they might think the best chain product for them is. The brand of drivetrain you run will affect efficiency, as will how well a lubricant is applied and maintained. If you want to maintain the best possible performance, don't skip the re-waxing, cleaning or reapplication, and if that isn't for you, find something that lasts a long time.

Though no official industry test standards exist, inter-brand chain lube test result announcements can feel like a fight for supremacy at times.

It's clear CeramicSpeed is committed to testing and developing the best possible product. Whilst its product has competitive low-friction or speed levels, there's more to a good chain lube or wax than just being quick.

items.title: Pochettino expected to lead US in Nations League games before Manchester United move
items.author: Pablo Iglesias Maurer
items.content:
Mauricio Pochettino will lead the US men’s national team through the remainder of this international window, a source with direct knowledge of US Soccer’s plans told the Guardian on Thursday.

Pochettino has emerged as the leading candidate to replace Michael Carrick, who was sacked as Manchester United manager on Thursday. The Guardian previously reported that the framework of a deal had been agreed between Pochettino and United. The Athletic was first to report news of Pochettino’s plans for the upcoming US matches.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
USMNT coach agreed framework of a deal with United

United have made contact with US federation

Balogun: ‘I’d like to keep things the way they are’

Live news and reaction for Pochettino’s move to Man Utd

Mauricio Pochettino will lead the US men’s national team through the remainder of this international window, a source with direct knowledge of US Soccer’s plans told the Guardian on Thursday.

Pochettino has emerged as the leading candidate to replace Michael Carrick, who was sacked as Manchester United manager on Thursday. The Guardian previously reported that the framework of a deal had been agreed between Pochettino and United. The Athletic was first to report news of Pochettino’s plans for the upcoming US matches.

The USMNT face Haiti on Saturday and then again on Tuesday in Miami and Cincinnati, respectively, in the quarter-finals of the Concacaf Nations League. Pochettino has been leading the US through training at the federation’s headquarters and training facility outside Atlanta this week. The Argentinian has yet to publicly address his link to United, though he is scheduled to speak to reporters on Friday morning.

United have also officially made contact with US Soccer in an approach for Pochettino’s services, multiple sources familiar with the negotiations said Thursday. Pochettino and his representatives had already ironed out details of a proposed agreement, with the Argentinian keeping the federation appraised of those ongoing talks. United would need to pay a buyout clause of $10m (£7.5m) to hire Pochettino and millions more, reportedly, to bring along his longtime assistant coaching staff, who are also expected to make the move.

At US training this week, Pochettino’s players have addressed the still-fluid situation surrounding their head coach. Striker Folarin Balogun told reporters on Thursday that “If I had a vote, I’d like to keep things the way they are.”

On Tuesday, defender Antonee Robinson downplayed the significance of Pochettino’s reported departure.

“As a soccer player, we’re pretty used to sort of fast training environments and games … so we’re all very good at just focusing on the next task and about the next session or the next game coming up,” Robinson said. “For me personally, I don’t really look at it … It’s just focusing on we’ve got a game at the weekend and I’m going to do everything I can to be ready to play for him, and how he wants us to play.”

items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘It’s gonna be hard to find minutes at times for Mikal’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
The Cavaliers did on Wednesday what they do best: win meaningless, regular-season games.

The Knicks, meanwhile, handed out a dub and ate a loss on purpose on their way to find their best-working lineups for when winning, you know, actually matters.

Here’s the latest from MSG on a rare off day.

“We’ll learn from this game, and keep it moving.”

On why Bridges remains a starter despite his shooting slump:

“Mikal is a starter. And so it’s not a question of that. He’s like a lot of players: They’ve had their good moments and their not so good moments. And Mikal has a proven track record of playing at a pretty high level as a starter in this league.

“So, for me to make a quote-unquote ‘panic decision’ and change it right now — we’re 10 games in or whatever we are. I’m not feeling it. So I’m good.”

On the Knicks’ defensive physicality and ability to defend without fouling:

“Just our level of physicality. Our level of physicality without fouling. Because you can be over the top, grabbing and pushing and holding, but our guys, they’re doing their work early. They’re doing their work early and they’re being real physical about it without putting their hands on guys. When you do that and you do that for close to 48 minutes, you usually get good results. And our guys are doing it.”

On the defensive intensity of Landry Shamet and Miles McBride:

“I think our physicality on the defensive end of the floor is at a pretty high level. And they [are doing] it the right way. They’re doing it without fouling, which is a lot of fun to watch. The point of attack with Landry and Deuce, especially, on the ball, is unbelievable.”

On Josh Hart’s perimeter defense and the importance of his return:

“He’s tremendous on the ball. In pick-and-roll situations, we always want our point of confrontation, especially against guys that shoot the ball at the 3-point line, Josh is really good at that. He’s really good at leading with his chest. And he’s strong. He’s a strong guy that knows the league, he knows the players very well.

“His impact when it comes to guarding the ball, on the perimeter especially, is something that you always miss.”

On the Knicks’ defensive communication, rebounding and improved pick-and-roll coverage:

“Their level of communication is high. Their ability to box out is high. Their ability to get back in transition is high. We were hurting in the pick-and-roll game defensively, but we’ve done a better job because the point of attack has been good and our guy guarding the screener has been great, too.”

On Mikal Bridges and Josh Hart losing minutes to Shamet and McBride:

“It’s gonna be hard to find minutes at times for Mikal. And maybe even at times for Josh. Because those two guys [McBride and Shamet] are playing at a pretty high level.

“Part of it is we got two guys that are playing really well in Landry and Deuce. And so it’s hard. It’s going to be hard to find minutes at times for Mikal — and maybe even at times for Josh, because those two guys are playing at a pretty high level, and not just on the offense of the floor but defensively, too.”

On the Knicks’ defensive struggles against Cleveland and his decision to keep playing Shamet and McBride:

“I mean, this is one of our worst defensive games overall that we’ve had. In the past five or six games we’ve been playing really well at that end of the floor, but they got loose tonight.

“And Landry and Deuce have been a big part of what we’ve done defensively. So if they’re playing at a high level, I’ve? got to keep trying to find ways to get those guys on the floor.”

On taking responsibility for keeping the Knicks in their defensive blitz against Donovan Mitchell too long:

“We blitzed Donovan in the second half and that fourth quarter. Give Donovan credit, he did a nice job making the right play out of it. … I kept us in the blitz a little too long, and I should have taken us out of the blitz. That part is on me.

“I kept us in the blitz a little too long. I should have taken us out of the blitz. So that part is on me and I gotta be better helping our group in that area.”

On the Knicks’ curious lack of free-throw attempts:

“[Cleveland] had 14 more free-throw attempts than us, four more offensive rebounds than us and two less turnovers. When that happens versus a good team, it’s gonna be hard to win the game.

“At one time, the free-throw advantage was 18-3. That’s not why we lost the game, but you just hope to get a little bit better whistle when you’re playing a good team like that, because it’s already hard enough to go win a game.”

On Brunson receiving no free-throw attempts despite playing nearly 35 minutes:

“Jalen plays 34 minutes or almost 35 minutes and he has zero free-throw attempts. That’s pretty alarming. I’m not sure how or why it’s that way. I know at one time, the free throw advantage was 18-3. That’s not why we lost the game, but you just hope to get a little bit better whistle when you’re playing a good team like that, because it’s already hard enough to go win a game. That was part of the reason why we lost the possession game. … James Harden had a great game as well. James shot as many free throws as our whole team.”

On Andre Drummond helping replace Mitchell Robinson’s offensive rebounding:

“Andre’s done a fantastic job in that area, as an individual. He’s not Mitch, nobody would compare him to Mitch, but he’s brought a dimension to the table that we really like. He’s always been a great offensive rebounder, and he’s showing it now as an individual.”

On the Knicks’ assistant coaches emphasizing offensive rebounding and transition defense:

“They’re handling the offensive duties and they’ve been emphasizing the crash areas. And they’ve done a great job — a fantastic job — of coaching our group, in that area. So our guys have a really good understanding of when to go and when not to go and how to go so we don’t get beat in transition.”

On the Knicks failing to execute in crucial moments against Cleveland:

“We were in it. But just timely stops and timely buckets were needed.”

On Cleveland’s defensive adjustments and his failure to respond quickly enough:

“You gotta give them a lot of credit. It’s something I’ll be a little more prepared for. I just didn’t adjust in-game as fast as I wanted to. I was still able to make plays, but not enough to win.”

On needing to be more aggressive even if it means making mistakes:

“From how we started the game to how we finished it, just from my end, I can’t be hesitant. I can’t be a little stagnant at times. It puts my team at a disadvantage, so I just have to be more aggressive in my mistakes, if I’m making any. I just need to have a little more aggression.”

On supporting Mikal Bridges despite his struggles and criticism from outside the team:

“No matter what’s going on, with what people are saying or anything, the people in this room have his back night in and night out. We see the work he puts into his game. We see the time that he puts in. When you’re doing the right things day in and day out, things will eventually fall in your favor. So just giving him support, giving him confidence every single day, regardless of what the noise is on the outside. That’s our brother, and we’re going to keep it that way.”

On controlling what he can after receiving no free-throw attempts against Cleveland:

“I just gotta control what I can control, and keep it at that.”

On taking greater rebounding responsibility following Mitchell Robinson’s departure:

“When you lose a great offensive rebounder like Mitchell Robinson, you got to pick up the slack. Of course, we have one of the best rebounders of the generation in Andre Drummond. But I want to do my part, and one of the ways I can impact winning and help our team tremendously on a nightly basis is make sure they don’t get second-chance points and also we get second-chance points.”

On the difficulty of defending James Harden after his 32-point performance:

“MVP, scoring champ. He’s a tough matchup for anybody in this league. You gotta tip your hat to him.”

On the uncalled goaltending on Peyton Watson’s block:

“I thought it was a goaltend. The guys behind the bench said that as well.”

On James Harden and Donovan Mitchell adjusting to the Knicks’ defensive blitz:

“James has been doing this a long time. Donovan’s been doing this a long time. They probably got a little comfortable. At the end of the day, it was a one-possession game, and we could have shored up a few things, probably, that would have helped us keep it a little tighter and given us a chance to win. But give them credit, because they knew what we were doing and took advantage of it.”

On his offensive rebounding prowess:

“I just got a knack for it.”

On the Knicks collectively replacing Mitchell Robinson’s offensive rebounding contributions:

“I think a lot of that is effort. And just doing it. A lot of us are crashing. You see guys like Deuce going in for those plays. Everybody, honestly. Picking up where we left off last year. We had a guy (Robinson) who was able to grab a lot of offensive boards, get us extra possessions. So all of us had to kind of step up and do that. But Dre has been doing a great job of rebounding, getting us extra possessions. Kicking it out and finding his way.”
